speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: All four tell us how different societies deal with race and religion.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Is there a larger picture showing interconnections among the four events?

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I will suggest to this House that there is such a larger picture, with possible lessons.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: This is an issue of considerable consequence to our society.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I, therefore, propose to make a Ministerial Statement and it is important that we hear Members of Parliament.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I will move a Motion later for my Statement to be considered by Parliament and that will allow Members of Parliament to speak on the Statement.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I hope that we can reach some level of clarity, agreement, on how we should frame, apply our rules on speech, so as to maintain racial, religious harmony.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: But one point to note, as a matter of record, regulation of content of entertainment, in general, is one of the Ministry of Communications and Information's (MCI's) important functions.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: My Ministry as a whole, and the Internal Security Department (ISD), in particular, spend a lot of time on this.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, my speech will focus on this latter aspect: hate speech, racial and religious harmony.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: First, I will deal with what hate speech is.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I will share using research in neuroscience how hate speech interacts with the brain, how logic and reasoning are ineffective.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Second, I will touch on the experience of other countries, how they have attempted to deal with hate speech.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Third, l will discuss offensive speech as opposed to hate speech and our approach towards it.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Fourth, I will discuss the Christchurch shooting and the lessons that we can learn from it.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Fifth, I will discuss specifically the cancellation of the Watain concert.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Sixth, I will deal with the arguments that have been made against our approach in dealing with offensive speech.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And finally, I will discuss the role of social media in propagating hate speech.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I think this has been discussed, some specific slides.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Assuming we do, then we have to consider: first, the degree to which hate speech can impact on racial and religious harmony; second, the steps that should be taken to deal with hate speech; and third, the continuum between hate speech and speech which is offensive on race and religion.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, what do we do about offensive speech?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It has been defined as "all forms of expression which spread, incite, promote or justify racial hatred, xenophobia, or other forms of hatred based on intolerance." It can fall into different categories on different platforms.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: For example, religious hate speech can be very powerful; political hate speech can be very powerful, especially if the politician is charismatic.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It can be in general discourse, in the mass media.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It can be as part of entertainment like music, theatre.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Look at Tab 1, hate speech leads to deep social divides.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It normalises behaviour which we will otherwise consider unacceptable.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It engages the amygdala, the brain centre for perception of threat.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Once that is done, it is harder for people to control their emotions and think before they act.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: People do not have to be extremists to be moved to violence by incendiary rhetoric.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Studies show just about any person could be susceptible under the right conditions.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: A psychologist from Princeton has shown that distrust of an out-group is linked to anger and impulses towards violence against that group.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Most people, most of us, are moral creatures.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, you picture morality as being in a gear.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: At times, it can get disengaged and set to neutral.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Morality can get disengaged when we redefine our actions as honourable and we believe that what we are doing is a matter of honour.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We believe the victims are deserving of their punishment – they are an out-group, and not quite human.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Distrust and contempt against the out-group can be built up.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Once it is normalised, dehumanisation of the out-group is very difficult to reverse.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Of course, a classic and extreme example is the Holocaust – how hate speech was used to mobilise an entire population to commit terrible crimes.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Jews were considered vermin by Nazi Germany, requiring fumigation by the Aryan state.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: A Hutu mother beat to death a child who lived next door because the government had told her Tutsis were her enemies, even as the child was looking at her, with its innocent eyes and they had grown up next door to each other.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: She justified the slaughter as "doing a favour" to the child because he had already been orphaned because the parents had been killed.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You have Pakistan: the concept of honour, shame involved.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If you are a true "Muslim", a “hero", then you will be a person who has the courage to defend Islam and the Prophet by killing "kafirs".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And that happened to the former Governor of Punjab, Salman Taseer, who was assassinated by his own security officer because he took positions which were considered against Islam.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You have Sri Lanka where Buddhist priests painted a picture of Buddhism as being under threat and promoted hate and violence.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Group's leader, Gnanasara Thero, suggested Halal certification is an "evil conspiracy", "spreading across the island in various guises, casting its dark shadow." So, one could ask: what do these countries have to do with Singapore?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Sri Lanka was ahead of Singapore in most indices in the late 1950s.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Why is it that religious leaders in Singapore do not say these things?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In fact, in Singapore, even the population opposes religious leaders saying these things.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I will show Members a survey which shows that.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is because of our laws and, over the last 54 years, the many, many things we have done to try and build a society based on mutual respect and harmony.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Hate speech was directed at the Muslim Rohingyas.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The leader of one of the movements called mosques "enemy bases", urged Buddhists to boycott Muslim businesses and not have interfaith marriages.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: When you have this situation, logic, reason will not work because an entire architecture of hate has been built up.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The marketplace of ideas does not work in these circumstances.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You take a place where you can expect to see crimes against refugees – in fact, there have been crimes against refugees – but where hate speech becomes limited for a period of time, that violence decreased sharply.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is on the screen but it makes a point – hate speech creates "a pressure to take immediate action and it creates fertile soil for militancy and violence." The rest of it is on the screen.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Let us look at songs which spread hate.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Studies have shown that music can create powerful emotions in the listener.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Listening to violent music stimuli, even without lyrics or videos, can cause greater aggression than listening to no music at all.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Songs have been a very powerful medium for spreading hate speech. "Hate music" has been used to label, devalue, persecute, scapegoat particular groups of people, often minorities.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They use it to deny the humanity of African-Americans.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In fact, the way African-Americans are dehumanised is to depict them in drawings, with stereotypical physical features which rob them of their humanity.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Some examples of the lyrics are on the screen.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But I do not want to read them out partly because of the language.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You look at references to "niggers running amok", "you cannot come up here anymore because now you are faced with the nigger foe".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Hence, a lot more not mentionable, not least in Parliament.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In the 1990s, there was a study of skinheads in the United States (US) to determine factors that were able to distinguish terrorist skinheads from non-terrorist ones.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: White Power music was found to be important to the construction of the identity of the terrorist skinheads.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Members may have heard of the Malay Power music festival in Malaysia.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Malay Power movement believes that Malaysia should be an exclusively Malay nation, immigration should end, non-Malays should be expelled.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: A Malay Power band says this, and I quote, "the lesson that we can learn from Nazism is that we can take extreme racist action if the position of the Malays is affected by these factors." Just across the Causeway.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There is nothing special about us that these things cannot happen here.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In summary, hate speech denigrates the out-group and says the out-group is the source of the problems; dehumanises the out-group, making violence against them justified.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Christchurch killings were motivated by white supremacist ideology.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Prime Minister of New Zealand has called for a global fight against rightwing extremists.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Meanwhile, Islamic militant groups are using the Christchurch attacks to push their own message of hate, that the West is at war with Islam.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Before we look at Singapore, it is useful to look very briefly at how some other countries have dealt with hate speech.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If you look at the US, speech is a very high threshold.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Before you can prohibit speech, it must be directed to inciting or producing "imminent lawless action" and is likely to incite or produce such action.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, it must be of such a nature as to produce "imminent lawless action" and it is likely to incite the production of such action.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Even speech advocating violence by Ku Klux Klan is protected under their free speech rules.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, you see speeches which are anti-Semitic, speeches which denigrate African-Americans, the Hispanics, politicians who denigrate religions and ethnic groups.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: One example is Steve King, a US congressman.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He has praised Mr Wilders from the Netherlands who has, in turn, called the Prophet “a paedophile, a mass murderer, a terrorist and madman” and has said the Quran is worse than Mein Kampf and has called for the closure of mosques.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In Europe, some countries there have broader prohibitions than Americans.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In 2018, the European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) gave an important decision.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The ECHR ruled that the conviction did not violate her freedom of expression.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It said the right to freedom of expression has got to be balanced against the right of others to have their religious feelings protected.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The German Criminal Code criminalises incitement of hatred against, or insult of, a racial or religious group.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The same section also criminalises the glorification of Nazi rule.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Just note that in the German Criminal Code it covers insults which may not quite be hate speech but could be offensive speech.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In the United Kingdom (UK), it is a crime to incite hatred on the grounds of religion.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The majority were on social media, involved anti-immigrant, anti-refugee language, racist abuse, anti-Muslim comments.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, the UK now finds itself fighting on two fronts – right-wing extremists as well as Islamic extremists.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The security services are investigating a possible contact between the Christchurch gunman and the rightwing extremists in the UK.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The UK's Lead Anti-Extremism Commissioner has said and I quote, "frightening amount of legal extremist content is available online", fuelling far-right activism.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: At one point, a preacher, Abu Hamza, was Britain’s most high-profile hate preacher.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He was finally convicted in 2006 for soliciting murder, inciting racial hatred in his inflammatory "sermons".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In his sermons, he described Jews as the enemy of Islam.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He told followers to bleed the "enemies of Islam".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They should not rest until they have created a Muslim state.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Britain, of course, has an admirable, long tradition of free speech.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But hate speech like this targeting ethnic, religious communities does not appeal to logic.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is not capable of being rebutted by logic.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The intention is that the recipients of hate speech should be filled with hate and they are turned into hate machines in the false belief that God requires that.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: How does logic and open debate counter this?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, Britain's lax approach attracted a lot of people like Abu Hamza who went about spreading his message of hate and London became a centre for many of these hate mongers.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Finsbury Park mosque, where Abu Hamza preached, has been described as a global magnet for militants.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The basis for the banning is that the manifesto tries to inspire murder and terrorism.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That has now led to a debate, "Oh free speech is being curtailed." The usual arguments. "Better to trust people to form their own conclusions than suppress hate speech altogether." The shooter himself confessed he developed his views from the Internet.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He said, "You will not find the truth anywhere else." The conclusion he formed: kill as many Muslims as possible.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We are told regularly that we should be more like the US and the UK, the Gold Standard for Free Speech.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But their experiences suggest that serious consequences can follow when you are lax about hate speech.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Our experience recognises that race and religion are fault lines, they are gut issues.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If people feel that their race or religion is under attack, the potential for violence increases.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If I can quote Mr Lee Kuan Yew, "No amount of troops would be able to stop the trouble if there was real hatred among the different communities.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The decisive factor would be dependent upon the goodwill among neighbours." We prohibit hate speech.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We also take quick action when there is hate speech and the speaker will be advised to stop.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: ISD will take action depending on the severity of what is being said and the possible consequences.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Of course, the person who conceptualised, crystallised our approach is the late Mr Lee Kuan Yew.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In 1999, reflecting back, he said this – it is Tab 3 in what we have handed out.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He talked about having done the easier part, getting people into housing estates, schools, putting them together.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: How it will be much more difficult to get people to accept one another and that it just takes one mishap.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And he talked about fault lines, and how it is going to take a long time, 20, 30, 40 years to work on this and why we need to find common ground, be tolerant, accommodative, take a multiracial, multilingual, multi-religious, multicultural approach and that one race or religion does not foist itself on another.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Prime Minister Lee in 1987 also set out our approach, that is Tab 4 in your bundle.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He pointed out the most straightforward way to destabilise Singapore is to have racial and religious discord.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He said never assume that free and open discourse will magically lead to truth and enlightenment.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Members will recall what I said earlier about logic not coming into play in this situation.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He referred to the 1950 riots, the 1964 riots, the 1969 riots and the Singapore Government's unwavering commitment in pursuing multiracial policies, taking action against chauvinist agitators and he said – this is an important line – "in race, we come up against atavistic human instincts which will take generations to overcome.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Speech does not fall into neat categories – hate, non-hate, offensive.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There can be acceptable commentary on race, religion, or offensive speech and hate speech.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Offensive speech can segue into hate speech and they overlap, obviously.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If Members refer back to the definition of hate speech which I gave earlier, it covers offensive speech, and remember the German Criminal Code which covers insults.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: At the same time, there may be factual observations which are necessary.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: For example, in a multiracial, multi-religious society, sometimes you have to speak frankly about the issues facing one community or another and to focus on the issues and to try and find solutions.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There may be a need to point out the differences among the races for a variety of public policy reasons.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The point is: should we allow offensive speech in general mainstream discourse, even if it is not hate speech?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Say, for example, you can regularly, in public discourse, including theatre, songs, politics, religion, joke, insult, laugh at, denigrate people of another race, another religion, what do you think will happen?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Take offensive theatre, the Ventriloquist Jeff Dunham, US, his puppets, include Jose the Mexican immigrant, Achmed the dead terrorist.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You can imagine what he would do with these.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He peddles in offensive views of various races and women, performs to sell-out crowds in America, he is one of the highest paid comedians in the world.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Members may remember a lady, Amy Cheong, who made nasty comments about Malays, their weddings in void decks.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You can see it on the screen, I am not going to read it out.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You can see how offensive and repulsive it is.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If this sort of expression becomes common in public discourse, what happens?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If we normalise offensive speech, after a while, the tone and texture of public discourse will change.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Offensive speech, in the long run, can also lead to dehumanisation.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There is emerging work in the field of neuroscience that if an individual observes another member of his own species experiencing pain, he would experience non-conscious neuro-simulation which leads to empathy.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But such empathy is only triggered when the person is part of your in-group.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Offensive speech, which implies that their target lacks morals, lacks intelligence, lacks dignity, in fact, is even more insidious because listeners may get a false sense that they are not internalising these sorts of descriptions because they are funny.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But you are being drip-fed the notion that the out-group is stupid, ignorant, immoral, sinful and, ultimately, leading to dehumanisation.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: When you think of them as subhuman, therefore, you may no longer be bound by moral constraints.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Subconsciously, the brain will not feel empathy for them.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is a slower process compared with hate speech.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Hate speech moves on turbo charge; offensive speech is on the same trajectory but slower.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If you look at our pledge and the ideals, "We, the citizens of Singapore, pledge ourselves as one united people, regardless of race, language and religion".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: How can we be one united people when everyday it is accepted that one race or another, one religion or another, can be publicly insulted, ridiculed and attacked?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Over time, the effect will be felt in every aspect of life – schools, jobs, neighbourhoods, politics.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This is an important point, and I hope this is a point on which Members in this House can agree.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Some people asked me what is the purpose of this Motion because they think that, at the end of it, we must have some legislation.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This is a debate simpliciter; we set out our approach, we set out what has guided our approach.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We want to hear the Members of Parliament because it is important for the next generation of Singaporeans to understand a bit of the history, to see what the ideals are, and how we should go forward.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If people want the approach to be changed, then we should hear it in the House and that will educate the young people one way or the other.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, it is important that we have a proper discussion.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That is the only purpose of this debate and Motion.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If we agree that there must be restrictions on offensive speech, then the question is what should be the extent of the restrictions?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: On this, do we think that Singaporeans are sui generis, that unlike others, we will not engage in offensive speech and hate speech because that is our inherent nature?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If we had not tried so hard for so long to keep it under check, through laws and work very hard on racial and religious harmony, will we have the situation we have today?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This is in Tab 5 of your bundle.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mosques are brothels", displayed a pig's head picture on a halal lookalike logo.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Gan Huai Shi, "Malays are rodents", ridiculed pilgrimage to Mecca.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And, of course, Amy Cheong again, she was a Malaysian residing in Singapore.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But I can also say, thankfully, it is much, much less in Singapore compared with other countries.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Most people will think this sort of speech as unacceptable.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Again, why have we not had the levels of such speech that you find in other countries?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But as I have said repeatedly, the legal framework is just the legal framework.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You got to work with people to also internalise it in day-to-day living, the lived reality of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This legal framework, however, requires us to assess, inter alia, the impact of the offensive words on the feelings of the targeted groups.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: First, we look at the words, the material – how offensive are they?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Second, we look at what is the likely impact of the speech: how would, for example, the community which is the target of the offensive speech react?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In a broader context, the material may be offensive for other reasons – social mores, values, child abuse and so on.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The regulation of content in the broader context is handled by the Infocomm Media Development Authority (IMDA).

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Are the words, in themselves, derogatory, offensive, insulting to a particular race or religion?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I have given various illustrations of offensive words.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Again, I really do not want to read them out.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Amos Yee, for example, talking about the Muslim community, Tab 6 on the handouts that you have, "They follow a sky wizard, they are dumb.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He is a paedophile", and he gives a four-letter description of Christians; described Buddhists, Taoists.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Of course, the US has given him asylum; we are quite happy about that.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If you want illustrations of offensive lyrics, again, I do not need to read them but it is in Tab 7, and it is also on the screen.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You have "Hozier – Take me to Church", "I'll worship like a dog at the shrine of your lies" and so on.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You can see there are plenty of materials all around.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, what is the second factor that we consider?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Consider the possible range of the different types of actions: religious leaders criticising another religion, telling his people that people of a particular religion should be ostracised; a political leader saying people of a certain religion, race, should not have rights in Singapore, these people are not good for Singapore; throwing a pig's head into a mosque.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The mosque also received a voicemail: "God is a pig.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: God is pork." It has happened in regional countries as well, throwing of pigs' heads into mosques; entertainment which is denigrating and disrespectful of a race or religion.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Assessment of the impact is partly subjective based on the nature of the words, the other factors, and the likely impact on the targeted community.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We also have to accept that different religions have entirely different histories, traditions, theologies.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, when considering impact, it is not just immediate reaction.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Other key issues are the security implications of the reaction.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And that can be immediate, it could also be longer term, by deepening fault lines, creating more tension.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That is the context of the earlier part of my speech.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I do not want to repeat all of that.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But as long as Members understand, this part fits in with what I said earlier.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We recognise their different histories, traditions and we make practical adjustments.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: On that basis, we take a practical approach, assess the impact of reaction of the different communities.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It often involves assessment of potential reaction of the targeted community when we have to decide to allow or ban something.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I will also caution we have to assess the impact, reaction of the majority in the specific community and the security implications of that opinion, which I have referred to earlier.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We have to assess where the weight of mainstream opinion lies.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We cannot be directed by the viewpoint of a person or persons who are extremely sensitive.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Really, the approach has to be guided by commonsense.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Again, I would like to hear from Members, should we change this approach?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There are two possibilities which will allow an absolute, objective approach.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Ban everything that is deemed insulting, offensive by anyone, or allow everything that is insulting, offensive, and I have explained why that will eventually lead to trouble.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It can be a bit messy but it has worked so far with relative success and with a bit of give and take.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, how has this approach been applied in practice?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is considered a literary work by many.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But we have allowed other books, films even when other religious communities were unhappy, based also on our security assessments.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: For example, western traditions accept wider levels of contestation.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And Singaporeans, I think, will agree that it is unthinkable to ban a lot of western literature and philosophy because some may find it objectionable.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: For instance, would we ban Bertrand Russell's "Why am I not a Christian?" because it is critical of the faith?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Would we proscribe Edward Gibbons, "Decline and Fall of Roman Empire", because it had a famous section detailing what he thought were the deleterious effects of Christianity on Civilisation?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We have to take into account the context.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, reaction of the community itself is part of the mix in assessing the security issues, as I have explained earlier.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The other spoke about "the evils of Islam and the malevolent nature of Islam" and more things.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The second video, again with your permission, Sir, Dr Zakir Naik, can I let that be shown?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That was said in Indonesia just before the elections for the governor.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He has also said Muslims should not take Jews and Christians as protectors or friends, otherwise they will become Jews or Christians.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: One is in Zimbabwe and the other is now, I think, in Malaysia.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Eight-two percent of Muslims in Singapore also believe that.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, for foreign preachers, we disallow even if they may not say something offensive in Singapore.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If they have been offensive elsewhere, their offensive teachings are available online, you allow them into Singapore, you then allow them to build up a following in Singapore.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, we do not allow them because, eventually, that can become seriously divisive – like not shaking hands, not greeting one another, not voting for candidates of another race or religion.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Sometimes, we will not know everything the preacher has said elsewhere.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And sometimes, we have to make a judgement on the degree to which what he has said elsewhere is offensive.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: On the other hand, I was concerned again about the normalising effect of such a sermon.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If we allow an Imam to exhort victory against Christians, can we prevent Christian preachers from saying similar things about Muslims, or followers of other religions?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Or taking some passages in the Old Testament out of context?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: What will then be the consequence if this becomes a regular occurrence in religious sermons of the different faiths?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: These things have a momentum, action and reaction.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Let us say we have this on a regular basis.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: What do you think the atmosphere will be like in our common meeting places?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He apologised to Christian leaders and the Rabbi of Singapore.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: To show that this was a matter of principle and that we accepted that the Imam meant no actual ill-will or malice, I met him openly, in a mosque, after his conviction, had breakfast with him before he was asked to leave Singapore.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In 2010, another Christian pastor, Mark Ng, denigrating Taoist beliefs.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Compared praying to Taoist deities to “seeking protection from secret society gangsters”.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Some people have argued that Singapore is secular.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, we should not be banning material that is offensive to Christians, offensive to others, because we are a secular Government.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: France has this ideology: the state will not intervene in religious matters because it is secular.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: French secularity means people can publish material that is offensive to any religion.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If Members look at Tab 8, you will see a series of cartoons published by Charlie Hebdo.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You have cartoons on the Trinity, cartoons of the Pope holding a condom-like sacrament and various other cartoons.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: When we talk in broad terms about free speech, people do not really understand sometimes what they are talking about.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: These cartoons bring right down to the brass tacks what we are talking about and whether you think free speech should extend to this sort of speech.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They used it as an excuse to attack Charlie Hebdo in the name of Islam.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: After the Charlie Hebdo attack, Mr Bilahari Kausikan, our then Ambassador-at-Large, gave a speech.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He said that the French state had hobbled itself by its own absolutist beliefs.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He said the state should be able to stop such publications.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The European Union (EU) and French Ambassadors responded.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They wrote to The Straits Times Forum pages.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They said that Europe did impose some constraints against the abuse of freedom of speech, especially against anti-Semitic speech.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In fact, one can add, in the vilification of the Catholic church as well.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Essentially, the French position is the right of anyone to vilify a religion is absolute.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think you can legitimately ask why should that right to publish override the right of a religious group not to have its texts, beliefs, practices, ridiculed?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And what about the obligations of citizens to preserve harmony, unity?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And if free speech is really absolute, then why prevent anti-Semitic speech?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Should we adopt the same "secular" approach that France takes?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Take a hands-off approach, allow these cartoons and other offensive material to ridicule, and hate speech directed at any race or religion?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It does not privilege any religious group, nor does it allow any religious group to be insulted and attacked.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It protects all, including minorities, from threats, violence.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It works closely with Inter-Religious Organisation (IROs), Inter-Racial and Religious Confidence Circles (IRCCs) and religious leaders to ensure a common understanding of what binds us as Singaporeans, that we all work towards religious harmony.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That is the fundamental assurance one gets in Singapore.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Does not matter who you are, what religion you believe in, you are free to believe in any religion, including not to believe.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That is different from saying that the Government should take a hands-off approach, in the name of secularity, allow people to spread hate speech, promote violence.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The French approach is illustrative of another interesting point.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is guided by a dark history that the rest of Europe shares, specifically, the anti-Semitism which led to the Holocaust, and the complicity of almost all European countries in the persecution of Jews during WWII.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Thus, in some European countries, it is an offence to even deny the Holocaust.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: These include Austria, Belgium, the Czech Republic, France, Germany, Luxembourg, Poland, Romania, Slovakia.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But does one really have to wait until a Holocaust type of nightmare against a particular group before you act against hate speech?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is not for us to say the French or European approaches are right or wrong.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Europe has a long tradition, a proud heritage.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But our experience of nationhood and the value system of our respective cultural traditions convince us the European approach will not work for us.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Now, Europe is grappling with other issues: immigration, multiculturalism and anti-Semitism are again on the rise in Europe.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Extreme rightwing populist movements, in some cases neo-fascists, are rising across Europe.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Obviously, the liberal values of racial and religious tolerance are not shared by a fairly significant number of Europeans at this point in time.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We have to decide what works for us.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Singapore is only 54 years old this year.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Racial and religious tolerance is slowly being rejected in older societies than ours, which claim to be liberal.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Prudent for us not to take Singapore’s values, unique and new in history, for granted.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The 2016 CNA-IPS Survey on Race Relations – it is at Tab 9 and it is also on the screen.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Sixty-three percent of Malays, 62% of Indians and 72% of others thought there was a majority Chinese privilege.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Even nearly 50% of Chinese thought there was such a privilege.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If Members look at another table, on the same tab, 40% of minorities felt that the majority race was demanding for more rights.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If you look at relevance of policies, thankfully, most of our citizens felt that our existing legislation, Racial Harmony Day, Maintenance of Religious Harmony Act, were very good things to have.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If you look at racism as a persisting concern, nearly half the respondents acknowledge the persistence of racism as a problem.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Even the Chinese, when you ask about their friends, they say 42% are either mildly racist or racist.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Studies have shown we react differently to people from different races. "The human brain fires differently, when dealing with people outside of one's own race," I am quoting a study on that.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We are more likely to trust those from the same race.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And I quote, "Shutting our eyes to the complexities of race does not make them disappear, but does make it harder to see that colour blindness often creates more problems than it solves." If Members look at the former Yugoslavia – Muslims, Christians lived side by side for nearly 500 years – and not just 54 years – substantially similar genetic make-up, shared history and Yugoslavia broke up: genocide and atrocities.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It just suffered its worst ever mass shooting.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Rightwing terrorist acted out his hate-filled ideology wanted to create fear among the Muslim community in New Zealand.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The response of the New Zealand Prime Minister and the people of New Zealand has been quite amazing, and there is much for us to learn from them.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Prime Minister embraced the Muslim community, showed that she sincerely shared in their pain and loss.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And the people of New Zealand have displayed great strength and resilience.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They have shown the world how to respond to a terrorist attack – not with hate, but with rejection of the message of the terrorist.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In Singapore, we have been building up the resilience of our citizens through the SGSecure movement.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We do not have the history that New Zealand does, and our population is much more diverse.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Nevertheless, I can only hope that, as a nation, we can respond in the same way in the face of terror.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: New Zealand has a relatively small Muslim population, compared to us.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: New Zealand police have, in recent years, taken steps to understand and engage their Muslim community.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They have even employed a number of our officers, for this purpose, including two Muslim officers from the Security Command who have relocated there.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The lyrics and the beliefs of the band denigrate Christianity.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: IMDA received the application from the organiser at the end of December 2018.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: After considering, MHA initially told IMDA that MHA objected to the concert.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: IMDA then requested a reconsideration of MHA's position.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: IMDA also proposed its detailed licensing conditions and requirements for the concert for MHA's consideration.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: MHA then informed IMDA that while it was still concerned, it will leave it to IMDA to decide on issuing such a restricted licence.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That restricted licence was issued on 5 March.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The initial assessment was that if the band did not perform offensively in Singapore, that should be acceptable.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Two days before the concert, MHA received reports of mainstream Christians being very concerned, offended.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: My officers met with Christian leaders, leaders of other religions.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Our Members of Parliament gave feedback – both Christian and non-Christian Members of Parliament, and many others.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: My officers and I take into account both the reaction of the Christian community, and as I explained earlier, it is not just the reaction of the community but the broader security implications of that reaction, both immediate and the medium- and longer-term consequences.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The band comes from a largely Christian country – 67% of the Swedes belong to the Church of Sweden.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: With the restrictions imposed, we assessed that the concert should be all right.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Our assessment was, however, different from what actually transpired.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, when you make assessments, sometimes, the reality will turn out to be different.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Why were the Christians offended such that they did not want Watain to perform in Singapore under any condition?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Because of what Watain stood for, its philosophy.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And you need to understand a little bit about Watain.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The frontman of Watain, Erik Danielsson, has said this about his creation – I am not going to read it in detail.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is Tab 10 in Members' bundle and it will also be flashed on screen.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But he said it has potential to attract fanatical people.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He says that they do promote lawlessness, violence, crime, madness, all hopefully for the love of the devil and the primal urge to express it.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He says, "We are not talking about ethics and morals, we are talking where no laws exist, and no morals exist." His views on Christians, "All our enemies are Christian sheep.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We go about doing our thing, pissing in their living rooms".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Music does have the potential to make people do bad things.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He was asked whether he feared that he would be misunderstood and that someone might go and start shooting in a mall.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And he said that, "That would not be a misunderstanding.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I totally encourage any kind of terrorist acts committed in the name of Watain, absolutely.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That is the way it works.” The interviewer then repeated the question, just to be sure, and he doubled down, "We have always been encouraging music to take a physical form.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: When churches were burned, to me, it is the very natural consequences of being the devil's music.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: What matters is the effect this has, and the effect that those church burnings had on the people was terrible!

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They were f------- afraid, they were sh-tting in their pants, because, according to the media, there were a bunch of Satanists burning down churches and murdering people.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is like holding your hand, the iron grip that takes hold around people's throats.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That is what was important about the church burnings, and that is what will be important any time a church is set on fire." And he said that, "That has never been a line that we have been afraid to cross..." Members can read the quotes in detail.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I have asked for the quotes to be circulated because there are people who said context is important, and I agree.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That is why I have set out the context, as provided by the band itself.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The band's lyrics are also denigrating and they are in Tab 11.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I am not going to go into them, but Members can read them with the background of the philosophy motivating the lyrics.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Then, Members may then ask, given all of this, why did we, in the first place, give permission for the band to perform?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As I said earlier, we thought that if we told them that they will not play any lyrics that are offensive to Christians and imposed other conditions, there are going to be about 200 people there, that would strike an appropriate balance.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But church leaders and others we spoke with, understood our rationale.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They, nevertheless, felt that we should not allow this particular performance.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, when we concluded that this was a mainstream view, widespread, and assessed the consequent security issues, we decided that the concert had to be cancelled.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Twenty-eight percent thought that it should not have been cancelled.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I recognise some Singaporeans disagree with the Government.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: For example, Ms Chew Wei Shan, a former teacher, set out her views quite articulately in a post.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Essentially, their point is that the Government is being "self-righteous" in trying to govern other people's lives and decisions.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Audience can listen to metal music without being influenced by a band's beliefs.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The National Council of Churches of Singapore and churches can advise their members not to go to the concert.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The argument in essence is: why should I not listen to what I want to?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Why should you, the Government, or the church, tell me what I can listen and what I cannot listen to?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The reality, however, as we have seen, is not so simple.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The larger picture, it is not about whether the Government should tell you what music you can or cannot listen to.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You can listen to Watain concerts, for example, on Spotify, at least as of now.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And it is not just one Watain concert.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We must allow similar hate and offensive speech, and I think if you see the lyrics and what they say, it goes well into the territory of hate speech.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We must allow, on the principle of fairness.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Logically, we should allow, based on the same reasoning.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But assume for the time being, we can draw some line that says "no" to political and religious discourse but only in music and entertainment, you will still then have a lot of hate speech in the mainstream through entertainment.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The question then would be: do you agree with the evidence, that hate speech, hate music, can cause deep splits, divisions within society, that it can normalise hateful sentiments, allow discrimination?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Would those people who are unhappy with the ban of Watain be willing to accept the following consequences of their position?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Will they accept that, over time, the fault lines of race and religion will be greater?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Do they accept that hate speech then would become normalised?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And do they also accept the consequences of that?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If they say "yes", I accept all of these, I still think we should have absolute freedom of speech, we should have the freedom to have hate speech through entertainment in Singapore, regardless of the consequences.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If they are willing to say, "I accept that similar concert entertainment attacking Islam, Buddhism and other religions should also be allowed." They have to say that.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You cannot say, "I only accept it in respect of one religion." And if we allowed Watain, do we also allow Malay Power music?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: These bands call for an end of immigration to Malaysia, and for non-Malays to be expelled from the country.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And they say they draw their inspiration from Nazi Germany.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Because if we allowed Watain, what grounds would we have to ban other groups with similar messages?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And then, do we allow Chinese Power music as well?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But if Malay Power is allowed to thrive, are you sure we would not have Chinese Power music as well?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If we can allow Watain and their lyrics and their philosophy, should we now allow the kinds of cartoons that Charlie Hebdo has published?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They were so repulsive that when we first want to distribute it, the Parliament Secretariat said this is too offensive to distribute in Parliament.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And I said that is the very purpose, to bring across to people the reality, what it is that we are talking about.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Should we agree to the mass media reprinting the Danish cartoons?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In 2005, a Danish publication ran 12 editorial cartoons under the title "The Face of Muhammad".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: One depicted the Prophet with a bomb in his turban.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Another showed him in heaven telling suicide bombers that heaven had run out of virgins.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Ambassadors from Muslim countries petitioned the Danish government to condemn the cartoons and punish the responsible parties.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The government said it had no right to interfere with the freedom of the press.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: A year later, the Danish and Norwegian embassies in Syria were set on fire.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: A mob burned down the Danish embassy in Lebanon.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: What do you think will be the consequences if we allowed the same within Singapore?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: What do you think our Muslim population will think?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: What do you think will be the consequences for us within the region towards Singaporeans and Singapore?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I hope Members, when they speak, will not flinch from these questions and run into generalities on free speech.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You got to ask, in brass tacks: What do you mean?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If we do not, are we prepared for the consequences?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If you honestly say, "Yes, we accept all these possible consequences," that would be an honest statement.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But if you put it in those terms and that you accept the consequences, you will be in a small minority.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I do not think many Singaporeans will support such a position.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This is in Tab 12 of the bundle.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If Members look at Tab 13, the latest IPS Survey which came out just a few days ago, 28 March 2019, talks about "Religion in Singapore: The Private and Public Spheres", 65% of Singaporeans identified themselves as "at least somewhat religious." Forty-two percent said they prayed at least once a day.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That is a very high level of religiosity.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Eighty-seven percent of Muslims and Christians read religious scripts outside of a worship service.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Eighty-eight percent had at least some confidence in Parliament.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think that shows that the public generally believes in Parliament and the legislative process has generally been fair, certainly with respect to religion and race.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Seventy-seven percent said religious extremists should not be allowed to hold public meetings to express their views.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And 73% said religious extremists should not be allowed to publish their views online.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But I should add that of the younger respondents, 45% of those between 18 and 25, were more open to such views being published online.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That is another reason why we should have this discussion here and a broader discussion outside.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think the younger generation also needs to understand what is it that they are saying "Yes" to and what the consequences are.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And 88% thought a religious leader should not even point out flaws in another religion to the congregants even behind closed doors.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is religious, but Singaporeans believe in giving everyone their own religious space.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They frown upon conflicts, do not approve of offensive religious speech and insults.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They believe that the Police should act when there are insults or criticisms directed at another religion, let alone hate or offensive speech.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: These views have been moulded by our own experiences and our understanding of why we have racial, religious harmony in Singapore.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: These findings show the support of Singaporeans for the approach we have taken so far.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Some commentators online have also said dark suggestions of a Christian conspiracy, they have a hold on the Government; Government bowed to their power; over-representation of Christians in institutions of power.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They try to turn it into a "Christians vs others" debate.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I say these people are nasty, opportunistic and dangerous.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I made the decision in my capacity as Minister for Home Affairs, enshrined with the responsibility of guarding national security and religious harmony.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Having initially made the decision to allow the concert, we had new information on how the community was reacting.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If we were only interested in tactical considerations, we would have let the concert proceed.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But that is not the right thing to do.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The right thing – more difficult to do – is to cancel and explain to the public why we cancelled it.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But I should caution at the same time it is not possible for the Government to accept any community's viewpoint on all issues, on every performer, for every concert, in every art form.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We will give due consideration to the views of all communities.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But ultimately, the Government will have to decide, based on the principles I have set out.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I have no doubt we will have to make many more such pragmatic decisions on concerts, books, materials which some will consider irreverent or even derogatory of religion.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We cannot and would not ban everything, however slight the offence.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The REACH Survey that I cited earlier shows the majority agreed with the Government’s cancellation of the Watain concert.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But let us ask ourselves: what if the majority did not feel that something deeply offensive to a minority community should be banned?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The majority of Germans in the 1930s may not have objected to the vile anti-semitism of the Nazis.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But that does not mean the majority view was correct.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I hope we would always have a Government that insists on doing the right thing to protect any community in Singapore, no matter how small, no matter what the majority might feel.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The social media has fundamentally changed the complexion of public discourse.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Hate speech and offensive speech travel much faster, gain wider audience than before.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I had earlier quoted a study in Germany.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Social media platforms have shown themselves to be unable, unwilling to deal with hate and offensive speech.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They have not taken real responsibility for the content circulating on their platforms.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Using algorithms, they can deliver news reports that are likely to elicit outrage and responses.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I have put in Tab 14 some fairly offensive pictures.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They are also on screen – white woman being violated by immigrants and someone is killing her child meanwhile.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Not in breach of Twitter's Hateful Conduct Policy.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In the case of the Christchurch shootings, Facebook failed to quickly shut down and remove the livestream video from its platform.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But that is a small number, compared with the circulation on WhatsApp.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And Facebook will tell you it cannot do anything about that because of encryption.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think the Prime Minister of New Zealand did well when she called for social media companies to take responsibility for the contents they published. "It cannot be a case of all profits and no responsibility,” she said.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Australian Prime Minister has talked about imposing criminal charges on social media companies that are not responsible.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Prior to the shootings in Christchurch, it was said that white racialist hate speech cannot be taken down, should not be taken down.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In a few days, that position seems to have changed.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Our approach to race and religion has largely been successful.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The lived reality of Singaporeans is the test.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In the 2016 CNA-IPS survey on race relations, which I referred to earlier, the respondents strongly endorsed issues relating to multiculturalism.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And President Obama said this in 2015 about Singapore.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: One of the reasons why Singapore has been so successful is because we "have been able to bring together people who may look different, but they all think of themselves as part of Singapore".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He said, "That has to be a strength, not a weakness, but that requires leadership and a government being true to those principles".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I started this speech by referring to four events in four countries and asked if there might be a larger picture.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If you look at Tab 15, my speech has attempted to sketch that picture.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: On the spectrum of race and religious relations, we are in the positive part of the spectrum because of the way we have structured our legal, social framework and all the things we have done to maintain racial and religious harmony.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: What has been happening in Iraq and Syria is an illustration of what can happen when things go badly, not just in terms of race and religion, but also other things.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They are in the deeply negative part of the spectrum.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: New Zealand represents a warning and alert to us that even a country which can fairly be described as heaven on earth can suffer a serious attack.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It shows how hate speech can fuel crazy people.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And what happened in New Zealand can happen elsewhere.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, New Zealand is positive on the spectrum, but uninhibited hate speech can have terrible consequences.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Problems that extremism poses, even in advanced, prosperous societies, are shown up by that attack.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Integration issues in Europe are a flashing amber light.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And German Chancellor Angela Merkel has said: "The multicultural concept is a failure, an absolute failure." She was talking about Europe.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The former British Prime Minister David Cameron said: "We have failed to provide a vision of society to which   feel that they want to belong.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We have even tolerated these segregated communities behaving in a way that runs counter to our values." For us, cancelling of Watain was one discrete step.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Why we did that can only be understood by understanding the larger picture of why we are in the positive part of the spectrum.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And that is why we are different from so many others.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Our current racial and religious harmony did not fall ready-made from the sky.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is not part of the "natural order" of things.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I am sure I am not pronouncing it right.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We have Group Representation Constituencies (GRCs) to ensure minority representation in Parliament.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Look around this House: could we have guaranteed this number of Malay and Indian Members if not for GRCs?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We have the Presidential Council for Minority Rights which checks that Bills passed by Parliament do not discriminate against any racial or religious community.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We have protection of minorities written into the Constitution.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We have the Maintenance of Religious Harmony Act.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Everybody knows that in Singapore, we will have no hesitation arresting any bigot of whatever persuasion.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Anyone who burns the Bible or Quran or any Holy Book in the name of freedom of speech, ISD will deal with him.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We long ago stopped Christian preachers from evangelising insensitively amongst Muslims.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We have had a recent case in Clementi of an attempt to evangelise to Muslim boys and the Police are investigating.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We have the current harmony because we did all this.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We brooked no agitation on race and religion.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We refused to let the State bow to any religious or racial group, minority or majority.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: All races and religions are treated equally on the same level.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Most other countries in Asia, if not all, either explicitly or implicitly, organise themselves vertically on the basis of ethnic-religious hierarchy, including a liberal democracy like Japan.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Our uniqueness in this respect should not be underestimated.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Equality of races and religions is not the natural order of things.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I believe   has come to believe that this is a natural state of affairs… They think you can put it on autopilot.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I know that this is never so." Let us heed his warning.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Inflammatory speech inciting senseless violence shrouds daily life with a veneer of danger – a heightened tension.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Last month, on 15 March, the news of shootings in mosques in New Zealand caught the world's attention.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The rifles used to commit such violence were covered in white supremacist symbols.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Since February 2019, Christian communities in Nigeria have been attacked, allegedly by Fulani militia.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: They were shot and killed; their houses were set on fire; they were ambushed while trying to flee.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In January, during Sunday mass, a Catholic cathedral in the Philippines was bombed – twice.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The second bomb exploded while they were still responding to the first one.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The Islamic State of Iraq and Levant later claimed responsibility for the bombings.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Sometimes, the aggressive perpetrators claim that they are carrying out the violent attacks in the name of religion.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Sometimes, the attacks are done in the name of white supremacy.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Sometimes, there are other reasons, but just as no single group has always been the victims of such violence, the perpetrators of such senseless violence do not come from a single group.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The pools of blood in a bombed church are as red in colour as the pools of blood in a mosque that has suffered an attack.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: That common redness of the blood provides reason to argue that there are individuals from every group that suffer at the hands of senseless violence.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: No one group can be deemed the sole perpetrator; no one group can be deemed the victim.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Rather, the perpetrators are vicious, slithering ideologies which propagate violence at all cost.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Instead, the innocent can choose to fight back by deploying a code of rules governing the manner in which speech relating to race and religion is used.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Such rules, which prevent the proliferation of speech inciting senseless violence against race or religion, have the powerful effect of preventing mindless violence-based ideologies from snowballing into physical attacks on society.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: What this means is that this Motion cannot only be about deterring phobia of any one race or religious group.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Instead, it should be about deterring attacks on all innocent people, regardless of religion or race.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: What type of inflammatory speech should we be deterring?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Inflammatory speech inciting senseless violence against race and religion.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Because such senseless speech reeking of violent intent can propel people into injuring or killing the innocent.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: That gunman in New Zealand had a skewed morality.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But even if he thought what he did was right, such senseless violence does not advance his cause.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Because it attracts far more criticism than support.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Because a moral code which espouses hate and which propels people into senselessly killing the innocent is wrong.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Such a moral code is not moral; it is immoral.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: What we are doing today through this debate is building on principles that have already been embedded in our Singapore DNA.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Therefore, what we are doing in this Motion is reinforcing time-tested principles to deal with the terror of the day.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Essentially, we are debating about what kind of society we want in the future by building on the cornerstones of the past.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: So, I am clear that we should deter inflammatory speech inciting violence against race or religion.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: However, what I do not wish for is for the definition of hate speech to be broadened such that even a differing view, expressed respectfully, becomes hate speech.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For a robust and meaningful exchange of ideas, it must be possible to present a different view when this is done in a respectful manner.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: A respectful and reasoned differing view should not be considered hate speech.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For example, during the Nazi regime in Germany, any opposition was quashed and severely punished.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The student group called White Rose (die Weiße Rose) "published anti-Nazi leaflets, distributed posters ... in protest to Hitler's policies".

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Helmuth Hübener, a 17-year-old, disseminated pamphlets countering the Nazi messages of victory in battle and also that the war was unjust.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In trying to rightly oppose Hitler and the atrocities that were being committed by the Nazi regime, many Germans, including Colonel Claus von Staffenberg, a decorated German army officer who opposed Nazism, were executed.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I dare say that none of us in this House would support Nazism in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But it is still especially important that there be sufficient clarity about what hate speech is because the term "hate speech" can be understood very differently by different people.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is also important because harmony is based on mutual trust and understanding.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Building mutual trust and understanding may require the ability to express one's thoughts respectfully in the right setting so as to clear up any misunderstandings or misconceptions.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: That is one reason why we have IRCCs.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Hence, I support sections 8 and 9 of the Maintenance of Religious Harmony Act and sections 298 and 298A of the Penal Code.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: These are some provisions that protect our racial and religious harmony.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: A strong argument can be mounted to suggest that the element of wounding religious feelings in section 298 of the Penal Code was engaged by Watain's lyrics in the distasteful songs of "On Horn's Impaled" and "From the Pulpits of Abomination", quite possibly contravening section 298.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Furthermore, a good and arguable case can be mounted that Watain would have also contravened section 298A(b) of the Penal Code because it may have "committed an act which the band knows is prejudicial to the maintenance of harmony between different religious or racial groups and which disturbs or is likely to disturb the public tranquility".

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The band has been very explicit that their music is the "Devil's music" and they even call their concerts "rituals" which they perform using so-called ritualistic props, such as pig's blood.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: After all, the "singer and frontman" of Watain has said, "whenever people take part of Watain, whether they like it or not, they are taking part of that place, a place with energies that are very real and that come into being if they are called upon".

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As for "disturbing public tranquility", that can be found in the interviews, saying that "There would be no misunderstanding if their fans start shooting people." In an interview with Metal Blast at Bloodstock Open Air Festival in 2012, a member of the Band stated "I totally encourage any kind of terrorist acts committed in the name of Watain, absolutely...

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We’ve always been encouraging music to take a physical form, and that’s what happened in Norway in the early 1990s when churches were burned, and it happened many other times as well.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: To me it’s the very natural consequence ... in the end, being the devil's music." I thank Minister Shanmugam for stepping in and banning the Watain concert.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We must continue to have that conviction to do what is right, swiftly and effectively.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: One day after the senseless massacre of the close to 50 Muslims at prayer in Christchurch, I received a WhatsApp message from the Chairman of Al-huda Mosque in Ulu Pandan.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Haji Azman Kassim shared with me about how a New Zealander, Mrs Kim Forrester, turned up at the mosque that Saturday afternoon distraught and emotional.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Within her, she felt the need to say sorry for the senseless massacre of the innocent people in Christchurch.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Moved by her genuine emotion, the mosque-goers present relayed the information to Haji Azman who walked to the front of the mosque to meet her.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
