text: He shared with her that he and the mosque community were deeply touched by her sincerity, at which time Kim Forrester shared that the acts of senseless violence were not New Zealand, the acts did not reflect what New Zealand stood for and that she was sorry.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: With a warm heart, Haji Azman said that he accepted her spontaneous sincerity but that she did not need to apologise.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Instead, he shared that her act of sincerity builds harmony.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: A New Zealander, a lady, walking into a mosque a day after the atrocious act.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: She knew she would have an audience who would listen and not berate.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: A community who would welcome and not blame.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And why did Haji Azman, a senior member of the mosque, so spontaneously walk out from behind his desk to meet her?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Because he sensed sincerity and comradeship in grief.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: By a sweet twist of irony, it was Haji Azman.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: That, for me, is a picture of trust, and it occurred within an environment of trust, which is Singapore.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We will all share Iftar during the fasting month at Haji Azman's invitation.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Would we have that environment of trust if we shied away from difficult debates and hard topics in Parliament?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is because Singapore and Singaporeans are unafraid to fulfil those very duties, to carry out those very acts, that we have created an environment of trust and peace today – a constant work in progress.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In that way, Singapore is special, and it is one key reason why I support this Motion.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 4.40 pm.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended  at 4.17 pm until 4.40 pm.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Hate speech, regardless who it is directed against – be it fellow citizens of different races and religions or against other communities and groups, such as immigrants, those of a different ethnic origin, new citizens or even against those who proscribe to different life choices, do not profess a faith, or are of a different sexual orientation – ought to have no place in Singapore society, either now or in the future.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Hate speech per se tends to exist at one end of the spectrum as it usually hosts extreme prejudice or calls for actionable violence against individuals.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Christchurch terrorist attack on a mosque by a white supremacist exposes the dangers of hate speech that is directed at people of a particular faith with the perpetrator making his views known publicly before carrying out his gruesome act that was roundly condemned by all Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Workers' Party, too, condemns this cowardly attack.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It is telling how significant our own biases and perceptions determine attitudes towards people who are different from us.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Apart from hate speech, however, is a potentially larger category of offensive speech, not quite a call to arms and as extreme, but expression which is deeply abhorrent, insensitive and completely unnecessary nonetheless.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This category can potentially be made even larger depending on how quickly some of us get offended, making executive action open to politicisation.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Given Singapore’s open economy and cosmopolitan society which are exposed to both Western and Eastern views, attitudes to what some regard as offensive speech can differ greatly amongst citizens and even those from the same religious group.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Most recently in 2017, MHA released a statement on offensive speech and expression involving race or religion.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It set out the Government's position in managing issues and reiterated that Singapore’s approach to the matter sought to guarantee the safety, security and freedom of religion for all, with a view to creating a common space for everyone.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: While the Internet has been an incredible platform in democratising information and has been a force for good in many aspects of our lives from economics to entrepreneurship, the anonymity, immediacy and ubiquitous nature of the Internet have also given extremists and those who revel in offensive speech a powerful podium.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Combined with the political economy of social media revenue models and the unique heuristics of the Internet ecosystem that highlights the sensational, hate speech is something all societies are affected by, with approaches to address it differing even amongst similar societies.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Going forward, Mr Speaker, and partly arising from the online space, my sense is that the Government and Singaporeans will have to come to terms with disagreement and contestation on a wide variety of issues because of the Internet.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Many societies around the world are getting more religious, with many groups more strident in their advocacy.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In such a context, the balance between respecting individual views of a very diverse society like ours that hosts different mores, thresholds and tastes on the one hand, and the importance of a fair and even-handed approach in governing a multiracial and multi-religious society on the other, will become an important marker of a cohesive and united society.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This cohesion and unity will be in danger if the Government is seen to be straying from its long-standing approach of strict secularism to preserve the common space that must be shared by all communities and individuals, a common space that must ensure minorities continue to deserve protection and should not be subject to mob justice.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Our people will also have a critical role in adopting an even-handed attitude in living in a society that seeks to preserve the common space, and respect the fact that no one has a right to impose one’s beliefs on others.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The recent episode involving the black metal band Watain is a case in point.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: From public comments made by the Minister and IMDA, there may be a conflation in the public mind of the regime MHA applies in deciding whether to approve or reject the entry of a religious preacher on the one hand, and the conditional approval by IMDA of a black metal band, for example, which covers a genre of entertainment on the other.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It would appear that different considerations should continue to apply in each respective case.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In the case of a preacher, it would appear that prior comments, particularly on inter-religious matters made by such a person would be relevant in deciding whether to grant such an individual entry into Singapore.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Should a preacher have described those outside his faith or even within his faith in offensive terms, then a red flag ought to be raised, as the Ministry has done in the past, and the person prevented from entering Singapore for the purposes of addressing a congregation.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Unlike the assessment regime for entertainment, however, it would not be reasonable or rational to impose conditions that require a preacher to avoid speaking about race or religion.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: If anything, promising not to disparage other faiths in Singapore but to be able to do so in other jurisdictions would make a mockery of the entire belief system of such an individual.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In the case of entertainment or a band, the Government appears to have a variated regime in place, one which does not hesitate to prohibit, correctly I would add, music that denigrates other religions, peoples or faiths.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: My understanding is that this has been imposed in the past for concerts involving even mainstream singers like Eric Clapton and other black metal bands.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It would also appear that IMDA and MHA's assessment included foreknowledge of Watain’s reputation, the use of anti-Christian lyrics and references to Satanism in some of their music.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: On the surface of things, these conditions should have addressed concerns about race and religion since the application essentially involved an established genre of entertainment.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I should also add that I was not aware opposition to Watain was prevalent amongst mainstream Christians until revealed by the Minister earlier.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In rationalising its decision, IMDA stated, in assessing and classifying content for arts performances and concerts, it aims to protect the young from unsuitable content, maintain community norms and values, and safeguard public interest, while enabling adults to make informed choices.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Allowing adults to make informed choices is a clarion feature of a secular society that seeks to preserve the common space.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It would appear that the original approach taken by IMDA correctly sought to carefully balance the competing and legitimate concerns of various segments of society.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Ironically, the cancellation arguably brought far more attention to the band and their music than it would have, had the concert gone ahead.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In fact, for a period of time on Spotify in the days following the ban, Watain had more listeners from Singapore compared to any other country in the world.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Interestingly, in the comment section of the online petition against Watain, more than a few interventions alluded to why the Government was suddenly allowing black metal bands – many of which regularly host Satanic themes – into Singapore.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: From an online search, it would appear that even local black metal bands have been part of our entertainment ecosystem for many years now and foreign black metal bands have been allowed into Singapore previously.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For example, a band known as Mayhem are one of the founders of the Norwegian black metal scene from the 1980s, a forerunner of bands like Watain.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: They built on the extreme metal sound crafted by earlier groups like Venom, Slayer and Bathory.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Their early years were filled with notoriety – their singer committed suicide with a gun to his head, and a picture of his corpse was used as an album cover and they were also tied to a string of church burnings in Norway.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I do not think many of us in this House are aware that Mayhem actually performed in Singapore in 2006.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Deafheaven, a Grammy-nominated band, but derided by old metal heads as a "hipster" band, also played in Singapore in 2014.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To that end, how will IMDA assess applications for black metal groups in future?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: As the 1989 White Paper on the Maintenance of Religious Harmony iterated, while the Government should not be antagonistic to the religious beliefs of the population, it must remain neutral in its relations with the different religious groups, not favouring any of them in preference to the others.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I would add that this expectation of neutrality should not only apply to religious groups but other civic groups and citizens in general in their dealings with the Government as well.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To that end, effective laws and an activist bureaucracy are only one aspect of the solution.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: References to the Golden Rule are found in all the Abrahamic faiths, including Christianity and Islam, and separately in other faiths and belief systems, such as Confucianism, Buddhism and Hinduism, amongst many others.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And even for those who are atheist or agnostic and do not follow any religion, such a moral principle, underpinned by mutual respect and tolerance, is one they, like all Singaporeans, I would hazard, would generously support.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Hon Members of the House, allow me to walk you through a few simple steps.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: You take one racially charged social media post, add a sprinkling of likes and shares, then layer on a litany of toxic comments.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Torch your volatile mixture with an algorithm that draws eyeballs and clicks.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: And there you have it – the simple formula for Manufacturing Hate 4.0.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: These are the everyday ingredients and steps for producing hate speech.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: How did these ingredients come so easily within the grasp of you and me?

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: The Minister has spoken today about the dangers of hate speech and its adverse impact on our social fabric.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: I will speak on how the digitalisation of our information infrastructures has made hate speech an increasingly lethal threat, one that demands a concerted response, both societally and individually.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: In a study by academics from IT University of Copenhagen, published in 2018 in the journal Critical Discourse Studies, Johan Farkas, Jannick Schou and Christina Neumayer studied fake Muslim pages on Facebook.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: These pages were purportedly by Muslim extremists living in Denmark who were plotting to rape and kill Danish citizens.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: They were apparently also agitating to dismantle institutional structures and transform Denmark through the imposition of sharia law.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: By spreading such combative posts, images and videos, these fabricated pages quickly triggered thousands of user comments and shares.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Although some readers questioned the veracity of these pages and reported them to Facebook, the majority continuously echoed the antagonistic discourse pitting Muslims against Danes.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: The anonymous page administrators were also careful to delete comments that suggested these pages could be fake.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Through this systematic construction of hostility between the two groups using visually arresting and emotive content, the page owners sought to normalise antagonism.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: They depicted these two groups as being fundamentally incompatible with each other, thereby sowing discord and legitimising discrimination.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Platform antagonism is thus a potent variant of online hate speech that is facilitated by our digital information infrastructures.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Participatory media include platforms, such as Reddit, YouTube and Tumblr, that allow for the uploading and sharing of user-generated content.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: A study by Robert Topinka of the University of Sussex, published in 2018 in the journal New Media and Society, analysed user-generated images and posts based on the photograph of Alan Kurdi.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: This three-year-old boy became the tragic face of the Syrian refugee crisis of 2015 when his body was washed up on a Turkish beach.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: This poignant image of Kurdi would be repurposed and ridiculed in a community of interest within Reddit.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: The specific subreddit r/ImGoingToHellForThis had over half a million subscribers and claims to mock political correctness in the interest of promoting free speech.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Posts on this subreddit are patently and unabashedly racist and nationalist.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: In response to Kurdi's death, posts emerged that made light of his demise.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Using macabre humour, they denigrated immigrants from the developing world and poked fun at refugees.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: In so doing, these posts used humour to mask what were fundamentally racist and nationalist views.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Topinka, the author of the study, concluded that, I quote, “cloaks, including humour and visual remediation, can provide cover if not sanction for such discourses…  reproduce one of the most dominant and destructive political trends of our times".

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: I have spoken today about only two trends in our digital landscape that allow hate speech to run riot, but there are very many more.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: If I could ask Members of the House to reflect on your not-so-distant youth, recall how you felt when you turned 30.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: I reckon that you saw it as a major milestone, a definitive step into adulthood.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: You felt sufficiently capable to make a difference in the world and mature enough to tackle life's challenges.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Is it the confident mature grown-up striding boldly into adult life?

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: If the Christchurch shooting is anything to go by, I think not.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: A medium that enables a cold-blooded killer to broadcast carnage by his own hand to millions of viewers is hardly mature.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: A fleeting like, a casual share, a throwaway comment – all these micro-actions can come together in a digital patchwork to create a tapestry of hostility.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Social media and participatory platforms have made it all too simple to produce and spread hate speech.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: We cannot, therefore, surrender authority for our communication to technological infrastructures, even as hard-wired algorithms increasingly rob us of our agency.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Instead, we must strive, individually and collectively, to restore humanity to our interpersonal interactions.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: To this end, there are two things each of us must do – exercise rationality and practise restraint.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: First, in exercising rationality, we must confront our own biases and our inclinations to fall prey to them.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Recognise that we can be easily swayed by sensationalist content that is emotive in nature.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Resist the urge to confirm only our own beliefs, and remain open to a healthy diversity of views.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Second, in practising restraint, remember that online, even though we cannot be seen and we cannot see others, that there are humans on the other side of the screen.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Refrain from making baseless, inflammatory comments that disparage others.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Above all, do not condone or share hate speech.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: As individuals, we must also exercise rationality and be careful when consuming online information and interacting with others online.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Our individual efforts can help deter the widespread propagation of hate speech.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Until and unless such measures see the light of day, each of us must exercise rationality and restraint to prevent the rise of Manufacturing Hate 4.0.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The hon Minister in his Statement outlined the findings of scientific neurological research on the impact of hate speech on humans.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It accords with my own research on the matter.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The objective of the speakers is to prey on the human psyche to divide our communities along racial and religious lines by – and as said by the hon Minister – displacing logic and reasoning through desensitising individuals to verbal aggression, in part because it normalises what is usually socially condemned behaviour.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Against that backdrop, the first point I wish to make is that we must continue to "invest" heavily in ensuring that, as a country, we remain united so that such seeds introduced by hate and offensive speeches will not take root in our multiracial and multi-religious community.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The reality is that in this modern era, it is difficult to prevent people from hearing or reading hate and offensive speeches.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It is not as easy as turning off the radio.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Hate and offensive speeches, as well as fake news, assail us through so many platforms, many of which are from overseas.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We need to work hard on "immunising" our people and strengthen our social defence against these speakers.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In this regard, I will, shortly, in my Tamil speech, highlight how easy it is for members of a race to feel alienated by playing on ethnic sentiments.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I will, thereafter, in my Malay speech, highlight how regular outreach efforts among members of different religious backgrounds, such as through joining hands to celebrate one another's cultural festivals and help the less fortunate irrespective of their race and religion, is singularly powerful to guard against anyone who tries to separate us along racial and religious lines through hate speech.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: (In Tamil):   In any society, we can find some people expressing their views to the extent of creating hatred against others.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: However, we have to be careful when such expressions go to the extent of instigating racial issues.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It went viral in the social media and many Tamils came to know about this incident and were angry.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: However, the problem got worse when some people in the social media said that, henceforth, Hindi will be used to replace the Tamil language.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: They said that Hindi would become an official language.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Such hateful views evoke unnecessary and wrong emotions.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It was only after Minister Iswaran had explained about these false exchanges that many felt comforted.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: He also said that, henceforth, translations should be done in a responsible and careful manner.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: After Singapore's Independence, it was written in our Constitution that the Tamil language will be one of the official languages.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Even then, the thought of another language replacing Tamil has risen.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Many arouse racial feelings and try to divide our society.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We must courageously confront such efforts that try to divide our society.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: (In Malay):   People who are involved in hate speech seek to divide society along religious lines and try to create an "us" versus "them" situation.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The objective is to create a perception that one group within a society is different and more important than the rest.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In this way, the group that feels that they are superior will be insensitive towards discrimination and, in fact, commit acts of violence towards others.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Knowing this, if the bonds within our society are strong and cannot be undone either along racial or religious lines, hate speakers will not succeed in their efforts.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Here, I would like to commend the efforts by religious leaders in Singapore who place importance on cooperation with their peers from other religions in order to show that we are a cohesive society and are united.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: One example of such a religious leader in Bukit Batok is Dr Suhami Mustar, the Executive Chairman of Ar-Raudhah Mosque.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: For the past few years, the mosque has been reaching out to disadvantaged families in Bukit Batok, regardless of race or religion.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: For instance, the mosque organises activities to entertain families in Bukit Batok during the celebration of various festivals, like Chinese New Year, Deepavali, Christmas as well as Hari Raya Puasa.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: These celebrations are jointly organised with other religious organisations like the Catholic Church, the Taoist temple and the Hindu temple.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The recipient families, comprising community members from different races and religions, will naturally sense the close friendship among the different races and religions.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In the spirit of brotherhood, these religious organisations also help one another.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The congregants were able to perform their prayers properly and did not get wet despite the heavy rain at that time.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: (In English): Sir, the next point I wish to make is that, having regard to the emerging trends, especially involving the social media, there is a basis to consider strengthening the current framework.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We could consider adapting the provisions dealing with terrorism financing.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This will make corporations and people think twice before deciding to support such hate and offensive speeches.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In some quarters, there is a concern about the possibility for the wide-ranging powers vested with the Executive arm of our Government to be abused in future.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In fact, I received an e-mail from my resident expressing this point.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Last month, I attended an Officer Cadet Course Commissioning Parade at the Singapore Armed Forces Training Institute Military Institute (SAFTI MI).

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It was a proud moment for all gathered there, particularly the officer cadets and parents.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I was delighted to see about 10 religious leaders standing side by side and offering prayers and blessings to the newly commissioned officers drawn from different races and religions.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This has been a long-standing tradition of SAF.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The Chief of Navy, who was seated beside me, mentioned to me that each time a Navy vessel is launched, our religious leaders will be in attendance to offer prayers and blessings, too.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Having enjoyed relative peace and security for so long, we may be tempted to take such things for granted.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The reality is that in many parts of the world today, this is not at all common.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The peace and security we enjoy are a direct result of the painstaking efforts of succeeding generations of our Government leaders, fully backed by fellow Singaporeans, to ensure that we preserve multiracial and religious harmony.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In the words of the hon Minister, he said, "We took no chances." Our unity and future as a nation will continue to depend, in large part, on how we manage race and religious issues.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It is, therefore, of paramount importance that we continue to be vigilant and guard against the propagation of hate and offensive speeches that affect the maintenance of racial and religious harmony in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: In the early 1820s, when our immigrant forefathers first arrived in Singapore, they naturally formed enclaves based on where they came from or the language they spoke.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The enclaves were further entrenched by our colonial rulers who divided Singapore into ethnic residential areas.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The years leading up to our Independence in 1965 were fraught with many challenges that threatened to tear our society apart.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The social bonds formed amongst the people were fragile; the slightest provocation or tension could incite violent conflict.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Our students today are still taught about the painful lessons of the Maria Hertogh riots in 1950 and the 1964 Race Riots.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We nurtured a sense of community and belief in a common destiny, by choosing to build a nation based on justice and equality for all, a nation where you and I are co-equals as citizens.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: As the late Mr Lee Kuan Yew said, "Everybody will have his place: equal; language, culture, religion".

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The strong community relations we enjoy today arose neither by accident nor by the laws of nature.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We strove to enable every community to have its own space to practise its culture and customs.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: At the same time, we sought to maximise our common space so that Singaporeans can live, work and play side by side in mutual respect, sharing common experiences and growing a sense of shared identity.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We have a nuanced approach towards racial and religious relations.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Every Singaporean has the right and freedom to practise beliefs of choice, to enjoy pastimes of choice, and to appreciate arts and culture of choice.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: But such a right cannot be an unfettered one.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: For a small country like Singapore, how we exercise this right should also consider the impact on our fellow Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We live side by side with others of different races and religions, and in close proximity.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Thus, every Singaporean has to be accommodating and practise give and take.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: This means giving up a bit of one’s own space and comfort for others, but, in return, we can expect others to do the same for us.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: In Singapore, our Constitution, laws and policies have been the traditional backstop against hate speech and incitement to violence.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The Minister for Home Affairs has touched extensively on the rationale of our policies.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: But can we assume the absence of offensive speech or communal violence in our society means there is social harmony and cohesion?

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Mr Lee Kuan Yew once said, "No amount of troops would be able to stop the trouble if there was real hatred between the different communities.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The decisive factor would be dependent upon the goodwill between neighbours".

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Indeed, forging a united people needs more than just the absence of denigration and discrimination and more than law enforcement.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: For while law enforcement can arguably remove hatred, it cannot fill the void with respect and empathy.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: A strong cohesive society starts from tolerance and, over time, moves to accommodation.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: From accommodation, we progress to an appreciation of commonalities and differences.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: It is a process that requires continued effort.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: To this end, we have been expanding opportunities for Singaporeans to grow a deeper understanding of one another through honest dialogues, across a range of topics.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: For instance, Ask Me Anything (AMA) is a community-led series of conversations where different religious leaders take turns to clarify common misconceptions about their beliefs and practices, as well as engage on sensitive issues.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: I participated in one of the facilitated break-out groups and witnessed how questions that seemed sensitive could be asked and discussed extensively but calmly in a supportive environment, allowing participants to clarify their doubts, get a better understanding about one another without imposing beliefs on one another, and developing trust through deeper understanding.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The aim is to articulate a youth vision for Singapore in 2025 and an SG Youth Action Plan, which will cover areas ranging from jobs and employment to mental health.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We will continue to support and expand these platforms and spaces where our citizens can engage one another candidly, discuss their perspectives and, if necessary, agree to disagree respectfully.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Our religious and community leaders continue to spend much time and attention reaching out regularly to one another to build mutual trust and understanding.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: This is not only through regular conversations, but also through informal activities, such as the annual Harmony Games organised by members of the National Steering Committee on Racial and Religious Harmony.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Our religious and community leaders have also showed solidarity in trying times.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: For instance, after the Lou Engle incident last year, the Christian and Muslim community came together and showed how our strong inter-religious bonds would not be weakened by insensitive remarks.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Second, we must continue to appreciate how our different cultures and religions make Singapore richer and more vibrant.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Indeed, life would be worse off if our hawker centres all sold food of one single race, or if we could not sit together with friends of other races to eat our meals.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Fortunately, we can have food from all races all at one hawker centre catering to different dietary requirements, and together with our friends and neighbours of different races and religions.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Our vibrant and diverse arts scene also helps promote understanding across communities, through works that reflect our multicultural identity, as well as works that introduce us to foreign cultures.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Many arts productions, through their exploration of humanity and societal issues, also remind us of our universal commonalities while recognising our differences.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Whether you enjoy performances at the Esplanade’s Pesta Raya – Malay Festival of Arts, or appreciating art works at the National Gallery Singapore, the arts are a powerful platform to unify people of different backgrounds.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We should continue to celebrate one another’s festivals.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Those organised by the People's Association (PA) and IRCCs provide opportunities for people of diverse backgrounds to come together and appreciate our different music, dances and much more.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Third, we need to continuously build and nurture strong bonds with one another.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: I am glad to note there are survey results showing that more people are having friends of different races.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Students from different schools and different backgrounds will have common experiences, and bond by facing challenges together.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We hope that through these experiences, people will form meaningful friendships with one another, regardless of race, language or religion.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: At the same time, we will continue to encourage a more caring and giving community.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We will provide more platforms for collaboration, volunteerism and giving.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: To conclude, Singapore's social cohesion and harmony are fundamental to our survival, prosperity and identity.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: But more than that, it is a testament to how we have succeeded in making our diversity a strength.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Our diversity is not a challenge or a weakness.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Because of our different cultures, beliefs and practices, each of us is able to bring something special and make a unique contribution to the Singapore story.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We have woven a beautiful tapestry from many different coloured strands and it is what defines us as Singaporeans – a key to our identity.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We have no illusions that our social harmony is fragile and precious, and we must strive constantly to protect and strengthen it.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Ultimately, defeating hateful ignorance and building a cohesive society depend on all Singaporeans, not just the Government, but every one of us.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Each and every one of us can and must contribute to building a more united Singapore, by reaching out, listening to one another, and building trust, one encounter at a time.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Our nation will then always be a home for all Singaporeans, bound by friendship and a common destiny.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: (In Mandarin):   Singapore's racial and religious harmony is fundamental to our survival and key to our economic prosperity.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Mutual respect and tolerance among the various races and religions are already embedded in our national consciousness.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Although there have been no racial conflicts in the past 50 years, the global rise of populism and religious extremism has allowed race and religion to be exploited to divide societies.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Our community organisations must continue their efforts to maintain our social harmony.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: In Singapore, while each community has its space, we must also expand the common space so that Singaporeans can live, work and play together with a spirit of inclusiveness and mutual respect.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Through participation in shared activities and the building of shared experiences, people will understand and trust one another better.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: However, building social cohesion and a shared national identity cannot be achieved through legislation alone.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Our goal is to move from simply preventing discrimination, towards a people united in hearts and minds.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I support our Home Affairs Minister's Statement on "Restricting hate speech to maintain racial and religious harmony in Singapore" for two reasons.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: One, anyone who cares for Singapore will appreciate and testify that racial and religious harmony is critical to our well-being and that it must be rigorously defended.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The second is this: my belief that unrestricted hate speech, especially if it turns viral, can quickly turn one racial or religious group against another and destroy the very social fabric that allows each race and religion to co-exist in harmony.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I wish to make a few points on the untenability of unrestricted freedom of speech, the adequacy of the current legal frameworks and also to seek clarifications over a few concerns I have.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Proponents argue, "It is my right to say what I want to say.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: No one else should stop me and no one is even able to stop me for practical reasons." Sir, there are at least three objections against this argument.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: There are other values that we honour, such as the freedom of other persons to live without intimidation and harassment; racial and religious harmony; mutual respect; anti-bullying and treating other people with dignity.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Freedom of speech is important but needs to be balanced against other values and the interests of the rest of society.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Rights carry responsibilities and freedom of speech ought to be exercised with due regard to those who occupy the same living space as us.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Unrestricted free speech, especially hate speech, puts a risk to the order of society.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I remember what my friend, management guru Dr Stephen Covey, who is the author of the bestseller "7 Habits of Highly Effective People" once said to me.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: He was talking about Singapore and the issues of freedom, order and discipline during one of his trips here many years ago, and this is what Dr Covey said to me.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: He shared, "When I was younger, I yearned for freedom.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: As I grew older, I yearned for order." And then he said, "Now that I am much older, I realised that order is freedom." Indeed, the order in Singapore gives us the freedom to practise our culture and faiths.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Unrestricted hate speech threatens the very order that gives us the freedom to practise our ethnic culture and religious faiths.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Thirdly, even if restricting hate speech is not fully enforceable nor is proven to eradicate or reduce prejudices and discriminations, it is still important for society and the Government to make a clear stand in principle against actions that can incite violence, hatred and bigotry.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: For the above reasons, Sir, I support the proposition that hate speech should not be protected and ought to be restricted; and that unrestricted freedom of expression should not be supported.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Next, on adequacy of the current legal framework.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: When the Ministerial Statement was first proposed, some of my fellow Members and I had thought that there would be new pieces of legislation introduced to further restrict hate speech for the purpose of racial and religious harmony.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: When the objection to the initially approved Watain concert was first surfaced by members of the Christian community, there were at least, I think, four factors of consideration to just let the concert go ahead.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The track record of Watain and its nonchalance towards acts of terrorism and going beyond its onstage satanic rituals into the realm of lawlessness and criminal activity are, to say the least, very disturbing.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Also, the unapologetic and blatant anti-Christian views expressed on many occasions by the Watain's frontman calling all his enemies "Christian sheep who don't dare to confront their enemy" and his encouragement of church burning.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: They are, to me, highly alarming and offensive.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Even members of the Malay-Muslim community, including mosque leaders, have also expressed objections to the lyrics of the group and its derogatory views towards Christians and Jews.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: For that, I think an apology is due to the Watain group and the affected concert goers.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I have some clarifications that I hope the Minister can address.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: As the Minister has rightly pointed out, speech comes in a spectrum and does not fall into neat categories.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Whilst it is easier to identify hate speech, offensive speech is not so.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I agree with the Minister that an absolutist approach of the two extremes of either totally banning or totally allowing all forms of hate and offensive speech is not wise.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: But this leaves a grey zone which sits varying degrees of offensive speech.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Whether action is taken against the speaker depends on, as the Minister has shared, the degree of offensiveness of the words and the likely impact in terms of the platform of delivery, the occasion and the reach.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Where does one, for example, draw the line in debating or discussing issues, such as abortion, infidelity, lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender (LGBT) issues, which, to some, are rooted in religious principles and, to other people, are just secular discords based on how liberal or how conservative one is?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Where is the line between public discourse and platforms, such as private WhatsApp group chats?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Should Singaporeans be advised to err on the side of caution to avoid any potentially offensive speech that can stir racial and religious harmony that may just go viral?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: So, these are clarifications that need to be addressed.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: This is similar to the feedback received from some younger members of the public who disagreed with the cancellation of the Watain concert.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: They raised questions about the Government’s moral authority to police music, performances and artistic content.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Aspiring to have the freedom to express what one feels, the liberty to read and enjoy what one feels like, is seen to be a hallmark of a free and democratic society.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: There are also other aspects of freedom that I think are important.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The freedom to decide on one’s choice of religion and to practise it, the freedom to not be discriminated against because you are of a different race or religion.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: I am sure we agree that we want all of the above freedoms.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: But what happens when these two sets of freedom collide or are on a trajectory to collide?

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Some may be sceptical about why these two sets of freedom can collide.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: If one were to ridicule or taunt believers of another religion, he may feel he is entitled to his “freedom of speech”, but the recipient can feel that he is entitled to be offended.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: And what about the recipient’s freedom of not being discriminated against?

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: These are difficult issues and each party is entitled to their own opinions and their rights.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: If we leave them to engage in a public disagreement, this could result in an escalating crescendo of extreme views against each other.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: And what if this spills into real action in the real world?

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: And oftentimes, this ends up being the Government enforcement agency’s responsibility.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: If the enforcement agency does not act, the parties may take matters into their own hands.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The Government’s overview on music, performances and art is based on classification ratings, tied to age-appropriateness and consideration for public sensitivity.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: MHA is principally focused on public order issues and, with that, the maintenance of racial and religious harmony as it can impact public order.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: So, why did MHA get involved in the ban on Watain?

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: MHA does not look at music and artistic content.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: MHA took into consideration the lyrics, views espoused by the band, and whether this would be significantly disrespectful, in this case, to the mainstream Christian community.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: But I feel the whole episode provides a few learning points.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The fact of the matter is that MHA was principally concerned about the words and the message that were being put out by the band, and the feelings, in this case, from the mainstream Christian community.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: It was not a value judgement on the genre of music.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Minister Shanmugan has shared that bans on religious preachers in the past have been imposed on religious preachers across different religions.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: This even–handed approach is a point that is important to various racial and religious groups and needs to be repeated often.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: So, we should look at processes and see how we can avoid a repeat.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: On hindsight, we are all omniscient and prescient.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Enforcement agencies will always be the whipping boy because they have to make a judgement call.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: If there is no public disorder, they are deemed to have over-reacted.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: If there is public disorder, they are seen to be lacking in preparation.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Government agencies get no bonus points for active intervention to create a harmonious society.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: And, over time, a harmonious society is taken as a given.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Are we saying that society can magically chug along and, as active individuals in our society, we do not impact the course our society takes?

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: I cannot believe that, and I do not think our young people will agree either.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: We are actually making a stand, taking action every day, in the words we speak, in what we do and what we do not do.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: So, we need to ask ourselves: how do we want the tone and texture of discourse to be in our society?

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Do we want civility, respect, consideration in our general discourse and public expressions of speech?

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The tradeoff may be some restraint and the inability to be "spontaneous".

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Or do we want absolute freedom and anything goes – potentially insults, taunts, offensive speech, in the name of freedom of expression?

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Should different lines be drawn just because it is on social media, or in arts and entertainment?

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: On the one hand, we cannot have a free-for-all situation so that one can step all over another and expect the other not to react or retaliate.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: On the other hand, we also do not want a situation where civil and considered discourse on all matters related to religion, race or a group’s values or orientation be avoided or tip-toed around so as to avoid any possibility of causing offence.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: In fact, this debate we are having in this House, in a considered way, shows that such issues can and should be discussed.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: As long as we understand what we are trying to achieve, and how we can work together to achieve them.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: In the words of the great American singer and songwriter Bob Dylan, who won the US Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2012 and the Nobel Prize in Literature in 2016, he once said, "A hero is someone who understands the responsibility that comes with his freedom." His songs gave a voice to his generation, mobilising them and motivating them.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: And he understood the balance that even artists have to strive to achieve.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: As we aspire to greater freedoms, with the stability and prosperity our society affords us, let us also have a care for those who may be impacted by our decisions, impacted by our words, and also those who toil to safeguard what we have.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Our pursuit for freedom brings a lightness to our spirit.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: But let us not forget those who carry our burdens for us, anchoring our racial and religious harmony for the prosperity and stability of Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: It is thus clear that we cannot underestimate the influence of speech and literature.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Sometimes, speech and literature can lift one's spirit and give people courage.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: But sometimes, they can also give rise to hatred and violence.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: We have to be particularly wary about speech and literature that involve racial and religious discrimination.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Because race and religion are the basic identity of a person.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: If a person is discriminated or insulted because of his birth, background, skin colour, religion and faith, it is equal to questioning the legitimacy of his very existence.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: And this can easily trigger hatred and conflict among races and religions.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: How do we handle these speeches and literature that involve racial and religious discrimination?

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Fortunately, Singapore has, since the early days of its Independence, established racial and religious harmony as the pillar of our society, based on our own experience, lessons drawn from other countries and the understanding of human nature.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: However, besides laws, I think the more important question is whether each and every Singaporean has got enough sensitivity towards racial and religious discrimination.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Can we practise what we believe in our daily lives to fulfil our commitment to social harmony, and strike a balance between personal freedom and the freedom of others?

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Some may say, I am not a terrorist, I just want to listen to some music and watch some videos.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Some contents may contain racial and religious discrimination, but I can discern good from bad, I will not become a terrorist.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Can the Government have some confidence in me and not interfere with my freedom?

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: To this question, what I will say is that when racial and religious discrimination creeps into the public view through various media, you may not be hurt, but the dignity of some other people may have already been hurt.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: This is like someone insulting and bullying you, then putting a video of his action on the web.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Do not do unto others what you will not want others to do to you.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: We all hope that we live in a caring and courteous society, not one that is full of hatred and conflict.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Racial discrimination and religious discrimination, be it in the form of words or actions, may not have hurt you, but it may have hurt other Singaporeans.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: When we see such words or actions, we should not remain an indifferent bystander.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: We should step forward, express our position and stop them.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: As members of the Chinese community, if we do not step forward and stand up for our Christian or Muslim friends today, we may be the one who would be hurt tomorrow.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: If we look at tragedies that have happened in our neighbouring countries, we will know that ethnic genocide may not be very far from us.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: As a Singaporean, I would like to thank the Pioneer Generation for creating a harmonious environment.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Racial and religious harmony need our continuous effort to maintain.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Although Singapore may look peaceful now, it does not mean that we can lower our guard and be indifferent to it.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: When one of us steps forward to defend our social harmony, we should support him and be grateful for his courage and sense of responsibility.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: As a mother, I hope that Singapore has a peaceful future.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: I also hope that the younger generation of Singaporeans will work together with me to create a beautiful world without racial discrimination, religious discrimination, hatred or violence for our next generation.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: The multicultural diversity in Singapore is something precious we need to protect.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: Music that promotes hate against one group and potentially divides society need to be tightly regulated.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: Last-minute changes of decisions are also not ideal and should be kept to a minimum.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: Creative expression does need space to flourish and a willingness to challenge boundaries.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: While we must be responsible for what we say or do in the public arena, we also need to understand creative expressions often should not be taken literally.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: Three, as society matures and the populace becomes more educated, I hope the Government can continue to focus on helping citizens make informed decisions and appreciating the diversity of creative expressions.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: In the sphere of arts, culture and entertainment, there will always be a diversity of world views and values represented.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: I am sure Singaporeans want to keep the diversity of choices they now have, even as we shield the vulnerable and the young from hateful and divisive messages.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: (In Mandarin):   	Making Arts and Culture for Harmony.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: A Zaobao report on 24 March 2019 pointed out aptly that "by seeking agreement while shelving differences, Singapore uses the advantage of a multicultural society to draw on one another's strengths and build resilience among its citizens, so that it can face challenges brought about by an increasingly polarised world, with confidence." Arts and culture play an important role in social cohesion by allowing communities of different races, backgrounds, religions and languages to have a common space to continue, combine and create valuable works based on their ethnic culture.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: Different ethnic groups have different cultural identities; we must first respect and understand one another before we can reach consensus in values.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: Hence, I have three points to make in this area.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: First, I hope that Government Ministries and public agencies can coordinate and communicate better.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: Agencies should also conduct more dialogues to understand from the organiser the content and nature of the performance.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: Second, we need more space for creative expression and challenge the boundaries so that arts can flourish and sublime.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: To create unique and forward-looking works in a multicultural society, we must think about and work towards tapping on our strength of "harmony in diversity" and endearing arts to the public.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: Third, as society matures and the populace becomes more educated, I hope the Government can increase the communication and be more transparent when making sensitive decisions, so that people can have a deeper understanding.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: I hope the Government can realise that art performances and production need a wider space for imagination to fully represent the essence and diversity of their content.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: Arts groups and artistes must build a high level of cultural confidence, cultural awareness and cultural responsibility, with the prerequisite of ensuring national harmony and safety.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: Arts and culture can be a centripetal force, allowing people from the different ethnic communities to work together to build a uniquely Singapore multicultural society so that Singapore can become an endearing and liveable home for everyone!

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: (In English): Artistes and arts groups can make arts as an integral part of everyone's everyday life, bringing together people of different races, religions and backgrounds, and creating a shared understanding across our various communities.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: As we say, "We cannot touch music, but music can touch you." I hope the artistic expression and imagination created by our artistes and arts groups can bring people together as a nation, uplifting our spirits.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: (In Malay):  	This is, indeed, an opportune time to discuss the issue of preserving racial and religious harmony in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As a Malay/Muslim and a minority in Singapore, I hope that my sharing can help to further contribute to and strengthen the harmony that we enjoy in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Hate speech or offensive speech occurring elsewhere will have a significant impact on us in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Hate ideology which led to vile irresponsible action hit close to home in my ward recently.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It has impacted a Malay/Muslim resident in my constituency and her family.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I visited her recently at her rental flat to offer my condolences and show of support to her family.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: She had just returned from New Zealand and shared stories, with her eyes full of tears and on the verge of crying, about her late eldest grandson, the late Tariq Rashid Omar, who was one of the victims in the New Zealand terror attack.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Her eldest son, Rashid, a Singaporean, and his New Zealander wife had four children, and one of them was the late Tariq.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Upon entering her flat, she immediately showed photographs of her son and Tariq playing football when he was a young boy.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: She mentioned that this could be why she was not surprised when she learned that Tariq wanted to become a geologist and had graduated in geology in New Zealand.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: She shared that Tariq was a gentle, caring and devout young man, a talented soccer player who coached a junior team and had immense potential with a bright future ahead of him.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: He was trying to help others during the incident at the mosque and was shot.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: On the day Madam Zawiah heard the shocking news, she was panic-stricken.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Her only thought was to check whether she had enough savings to purchase a flight ticket to New Zealand to be with her eldest son’s family and, despite not being fluent in English, she flew there alone.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Some of our non-Muslim and Chinese business community members and volunteers in Toa Payoh East-Novena banded together to help her in any way possible, including assisting her with the costs of the urgent flight.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But I feel reassured and optimistic that, even in Toa Payoh East-Novena, our community is aware of the deadly effects of hate speech on one of our own and have offered help.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, here in the comforts of Singapore, we, too, are not immune if hate speech on different groups or segments of the community proliferate globally.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We have family members, Singaporeans of different religions and races travelling widely and living abroad for work as well.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
