text: Here in Singapore, the social media and our openness allow us to be exposed to a myriad of information.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: What is important is that we exercise caution and adopt a firm stand against hate speech directed at any group or segments of society in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: (In English): My resident's story and the loss of her eldest grandchild is just one example.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But I hope it should raise awareness about how hate speech could have adverse consequences for anyone when we least expect it.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We are lauded as the model of social harmony.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But let me state upfront that we should not allow offensive and hate speech to be normalised in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: What happens in other countries is beyond our control.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In his Statement, the Minister posed a few questions to the House.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I believe the Government has been impartial, fair and just in applying decisions thus far.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But I think we can improve on making sure the neutrality of the Government in such decisions remains strong and unwavering.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The Minister has highlighted clearly that Government neutrality is key, and the perception of it even more.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: How can we ensure that neutrality remains so when future decisions are made?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Can we have a council of sorts, akin to the Presidential Council on Minority and Religious Rights, to advise the deciding Minister on matters relating to hate and offensive speech so that the neutrality element remains guarded?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It could help alleviate issues of conflict of interest if, in the future, the deciding Minister is of a particular religion or race impacted by the offensive or hate speech or ideology, in particular for future Governments.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In addition, hate speech and offensive speech apply to various segments, races and religions on either side of the spectrum, for example, the rise in Islamophobia globally and the risks it poses to the Muslim community.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I am sure MHA has looked into this and, while the financial cost burden may be there, I feel it is necessary to reiterate that additional resources must be added to our security intelligence departments to look at terrorist threats from both sides of the spectrum as well as rising Islamophobia, so that, internally, we have a balanced view of the threats that may hit any Singaporean, regardless of race, language or religion and take pre-emptive action if needed.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But on top of all these, what more can we do?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We must never be complacent and should embrace ideas that help to mitigate the dangers of normalisation of hate speech.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We have a high number of citizens who have Internet access and are avid consumers of foreign news and social media content.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: One is how we can build resilience in our future generation to identify offensive and hate speech and reject such efforts.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Second, how we, as a nation, can take efforts at all levels to reduce the risk of perpetuating stereotypes of segments by race or religion which can be used as fuel or seeds for hate and offensive speech.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Did we miss a step in our outreach to our young to educate them on the dangers of exposure to such hate posts?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I read about a school in Brazil where students are taught how to identify fake news.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Maybe we can apply a similar approach in our schools and tertiary institutions and use such skills to identify hate or offensive speech so that it does not get normalised easily here.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Next, the threat of terrorism from all races and religions is a practical reason for all Singaporeans to take Islamophobia, for example, and all forms of racial and religious discrimination seriously.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We would be looking at Singapore through rose-tinted glasses if we truly believe there is no racial discrimination in Singapore, or that it is so insignificant that we do not have to worry.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This absolutely necessitates the conversations we are having here.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It is not uncommon to find discriminatory comments often based on negative stereotypes left on discussion platforms on social media.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: These comments are not malicious to be prosecuted under our legal framework, but they demonstrate a lack of understanding and unfair generalisation towards specific races or religions.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: However, to minimise discrimination and pursue social harmony, we must go beyond restricting hate speech.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Maybe more can be done to encourage even more Singaporeans of various races and religion to have friends from other races and, most importantly, for sharing more stories of bonds and trust among the races more prevalently, in order to build up the trust premium among the different races and religion.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The risk of perpetuating of stereotypes is another issue that we should address as it can be the fuel or ingredient for hate speech and ideology.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: If we perpetuate stereotypes, parents, for example, can pass on this mistrust and the stereotypes to their children, and the cycle carries on generation after generation.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The mistrust and stereotyping will remain entrenched, never going away, unless we nip the problem in the bud and change these mindsets and perceptions.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Maybe these can be done even more at the grassroots level through sports and interest groups, for example, as mentioned by Minister Grace Fu earlier.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In Toa Payoh East-Novena (TEN), we have a cycling enthusiasts group made up of young professionals of various races and sports which could be a good example to form bonds.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We are trying to encourage more young parents to join these activities.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Through these programmes it is hoped that they will develop positive perceptions about their fellow Singaporeans, regardless of race, and hope they would guide their own children with love, not discrimination or hate.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: If, from stereotyping, distrust, mischief and misguidance among some people build up, then with the prevalence of hate speech and hate messages, the cracks can turn into chasms.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: And once this happens, what is not normal becomes the norm.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I note that with the help of the IRCCs, some religious organisations of different faiths have collaborated to implement volunteer programmes, such as the blood donation drive by Masjid Khalid and Heart of God Church.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I hope that such collaborations will be encouraged, as charity is an excellent platform to put volunteers and beneficiaries on the same page.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I would thus suggest that to create more opportunities for interaction, we can look into, say, a Buddhist volunteer who usually volunteers for the temple's charity programmes could work with Muslim volunteers at a mosque to distribute food to the needy or perform ushering duties, for example.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Hindu volunteers could put together a performance to entertain elderly beneficiaries of a Buddhist temple.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This is in line with the national goal of encouraging Singaporeans to be more involved in volunteer work.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We cannot restrict hate speech beyond the shores of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But we can denormalise it at home by making it not cool, by speaking out against it.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This is not because Singaporeans are immature and easily swayed by hate speech.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It is about sending a very clear message and taking a firm stand against something that threatens our social fabric.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Can we do more to help others understand why certain acts or words are so offensive, that it is not a matter of being small-minded or intolerant?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I wonder if we can tap on local celebrities and influencers or even more to help engage the youths and spread the message?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: On a final note, the Internet has become a toxic waste dump for hate and malice, and any news story can pretty much be manipulated to divide people, not to mention perpetuate stereotypes, too.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The Internet promotes a sheep-mentality that turns people into raging mobs without obtaining a full understanding of the situation.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I hope Singapore will continue to walk the tightrope with good balance to preserve the peace and harmony that we enjoy.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This is a never-ending goal that our leaders, religious groups, all Singaporeans must continuously strive for.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Everyone believes in the importance of racial and religious harmony.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But what happens when hate speech and offensive speech take place?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In this age of high interconnectivity, such negative expressions through messaging, music, writing and art can travel the globe at the speed of light.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The mask of anonymity and the camouflage of encryption further aid the proliferation of hate speech.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: A body of research and our own experiences had shown us that it is easier to pick up bad behaviour than good.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Thus, we need holistic measures to prevent a downward spiral of hate speech begetting more retaliating hate speech.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: History teaches us that in all communities and countries, racial and religious harmony is fragile.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Hence, it is important that we nip any threats in the bud as early as possible.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We cannot afford the escalation of toxic communication nor the contagion of acrimony.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The greater the number of Singaporeans and residents who resist and call out hate and offensive speech, the more protection we have as a nation.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: (In Mandarin):   To borrow a medical terminology, we need to build our collective immunity against the hate speech through the vaccine of building trust among communities to overcome ignorance and misinformation.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The greater the number of Singaporeans and residents who resist and call out hate and offensive speech, the more protection we have as a nation.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: (In English): We also need to strengthen our capabilities in dealing with three groups of people.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The first group is those who feel targeted but who may keep silent, bearing grudges.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Subsequently, when the occurrences of hate speech become more frequent, some in this group may lose control and turn violent to hurt those they perceive as perpetrators.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: How can we identify the silent sufferers who may blow up, and calm these "victims" before they make outbursts?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The second group is those who speak up.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, if they do not communicate in a constructive way, they may actually cause more harm and contribute to a more explosive situation.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: How can we help them to express and register their objections to hate speech which target them, but in ways which will not exacerbate the problem?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The third group is those traumatised by hate speech and related incidents.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: How do we help our people who have been traumatised by such incidents overseas?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: They incite hatred and even encourage criminal acts and terrorism.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Their hypocrisy and inconsistency between what they advocate and what they do should be highlighted.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Even as the group encourages hate speech and urges the destruction of harmonious and constructive communities, its members continue to enjoy the convenience and even luxuries of the products of peace.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: These include the infrastructure and the services of people from different races and religions working hard to provide them with clean water, safe food, reliable travel and electricity which make their concerts possible.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: There are inherent contradictions between the great and historic truths embodied in different religious and cultural traditions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: When these contradictions surface in public, people may and do take offence.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: This contradiction can only be resolved with the state promoting an enlightened and neutral secularism that respects all religions and races, but which also firmly pushes back on attempts to encroach on the public space to the detriment of all.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I believe this House accepts that every major religion has, at heart, certain great truths about the purpose of life and the way we should live a meaningful life.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Those who are non-religious also seek meaning and purpose in life.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: This is a natural response to the question of human existence.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But the problem is that all these great truths cannot be truthful all at once.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: And even if by divine providence they are, human practice inevitably corrupts the truth.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Because great truths compel us to put principles into practice, the end result is that offence can and will be taken.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Christianity would not exist if Jesus had not driven out the merchants and the moneychangers from the Temple and created the conditions for a social revolution.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The Protestant churches would not exist if Martin Luther had not published his 95 theses against the abuses of the medieval Catholic Church.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Islam would not exist if the Prophet, peace be upon him, had not put divine revelation into practice by mobilising society against the injustice of his time.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: All of these acts, while creating great religions, would have caused great offence to the entrenched communities of the time.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The problem is that beliefs and culture are not just private matters.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The world's great religions are great because they provide us a framework of how to live.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The racial groups that make up Singapore, likewise, have centuries of culture and practice which still guide modern life.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: And so it is inevitable that one man's belief or culture when put into the public sphere may give offence to another.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: A basic example is the prohibition on food, which can be religious or cultural.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: What do you do when simple consumption of food in plain sight – whether it is pork, beef, alcohol, other animals – is normal to some but gives offence to others?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: What about refusal to consume food that is thought to be consecrated to another religion or to be unclean?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: This is the essential contradiction we are faced with.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: A great truth that motivates people to live their lives according to a higher purpose must at some point face entrenched interests and different ways of life.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: As a result, many great truths when put into practice, will be regarded as deeply offensive, just as others regard it as the gospel truth.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: First, I believe the state should reinforce a secular public policy space based on the founding principle that we are a multiracial and religious society.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The public space is a common resource, a deep wellspring that sustains and refreshes the common spirit.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: If we had one overwhelmingly dominant religion and/or race, then the question is one of tolerance of minorities and not of what the public space should be like.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But as a multiracial and religious society, each of our communities has different ideas about that public space.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Our society must keep that common wellspring clear.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: This is so even when several religions or groups claim common cause.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: To take a current issue, many Singaporean Christians and Muslims believe that homosexual behaviour is offensive to their ideals of what the public space and the family should be.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: This is not the time to debate these views.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The point is what is offensive to one group may not be so to another.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Once that principle is normalised, no single religion or racial group can feel safe.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Next, our religious and racial communities must accept that they have a role to play in balancing the public exercise of their faith with an understanding that sensitivity bordering on intolerance will inevitably put each community against the other.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: While the vast majority today agree that our laws should not be based on religion, personal conscience matters.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Taken by itself, there is nothing wrong with putting principles into action this way.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: It is an authentic expression of the human spirit in public life.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But the question for us is whether we are able to accept and make such religiously motivated arguments without giving or taking offence, and whether we can come to a consensus to accept a settled question of public policy even when it conflicts with our personal principles.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: In short, any assertiveness based on religious principle must be matched by an equal open mindedness to accept honest disagreements without taking offence.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I agree that the Government must continue to pursue a balanced framework that takes into consideration deep-seated harm to an entire community and not just the most sensitive members of that community.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But what happens when the tenor of sensitivity changes with time and what was formerly regarded as a secular problem becomes an article of faith?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Even a balanced framework will be gradually driven into a corner where everything causes an offence and nothing is accepted, if our racial and religious groups become more intolerant over time.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: So, we are back to the deep question: who gets to decide if something gives offence?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I share the Minister's views that it must be taken outside to the public as well.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The state must work with the community to robustly defend the public space.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Indeed, the early Catholic Church, Islam and the Protestant Church spread despite repression because society recognised the great truths embodied in these religious ideals.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Academics, journalists and civil society alike need the freedom to ask and answer inconvenient questions about race and religion that may offend some.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Of course, some honestly held views today are considered so offensive that I do not think we will see them contested openly in the near future.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The issue of conversion is also deeply sensitive.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But that does not mean we should not try to advance the principle that intent matters and not just the degree of offence taken.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: It is the result of careful cooperation between the state and society.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But we should go beyond just taking community views or considerations as given.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: We must remember that while each of us belongs to minorities of our own, we share a common spirit as human beings and citizens of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: What happened in New Zealand recently at the two mosques was tragic and unexpected.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: On behalf of all Singaporeans, I would like to sincerely offer our condolences to the families that had lost their loved ones.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: May their souls rest in peace and in eternal happiness.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: (In Malay):   I offer my condolences to Mdm Noraini Abbas from Singapore, Mr John Milne and their whole family for their family’s great loss, the late Sayyad Milne.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: May the late Sayyad Milne be granted a place in the highest level of Paradise in eternal happiness.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: (In English): Mdm Noraini Abbas, we are with you.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore is with you and your family, as you mourn the loss of your beloved son, Sayyad Milne.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: The various events happening worldwide have been saddening.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Generation after generation, the words Hate or Hate speech have been very powerful, that causes one to act irrationally and drastically.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: It can be anyone unassuming, regardless of his race, colour or religious belief and, to a point of, in Islam we say breaking Siratul Rahim – breaking the bonds between mankind using fear, hate, anger, jealousy, greed and even innocence.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: This makes me wonder what is that trigger point that the power of hate or hate speech have over man.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: It can take over a person’s logical power of thinking and reasoning to reach a point of irrational behaviour, to hate and even to kill.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Wisdom is gone forever from their hearts when hate takes over their mind.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: The innocent bystanders, the innocent child, the innocent people working hard to earn a living to feed their loved ones.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: A wise man once said, "Tie the rosary beads too tight and they would surely break and fall with great impact uncontrollably.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Tie it too loose, they would also naturally fall apart.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Amidst the grief, despair and anger, the tragic event in Christchurch has created a cause for a deeper reflection of the significant challenges to extremism.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Over the last few weeks, many news commentaries and reports have discussed gun laws, the role of social media, white supremacy and anti-Muslim rhetoric.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: As a multicultural and multi-religious society, we have developments that have an impact on our social cohesion in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Positive and meaningful social exchanges among different races and religious groups create the foundation for social cohesion.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Like a rich tapestry, our Singapore story is alive only because of the fine, interwoven threads of social interactions.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Today, at the national, community and ground-up level, we have a number of platforms and initiatives for different communities to come together, build mutual respect and trust and deepen understanding about one another.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: However, as the Christchurch incident has reminded us, there is still much work that needs to be done.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Underlying tensions, prejudice and stereotypes among different races and religions continue to be a challenge.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Through my involvement in Roses of Peace, a ground-up non-profit organisation working on peace-building, we have observed many cases where members of the community have experienced micro-aggressions and discrimination.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: It is thus important that we face squarely the challenges we have and find ways to proactively address it.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: As President Halimah Yacob noted after the Christchurch incident, the most important lesson for us is to fight all forms of xenophobia and hatred perpetrated simply on the basis of a person’s religion, colour or creed.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Xenophobia and hatred can cut deep divisions among us and allow hatred to spread, and this cannot be prevented easily.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: As a community, I believe it is important for us to have honest and meaningful conversations, beyond the polite niceties, of what is going on.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Such conversations may be unpleasant at some point and to people in general, but this is an opportunity to talk about their own experiences, in what they face in life and to listen to others and understand and come to reach an understanding.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: By allowing for more honest and meaningful dialogue and interaction, we can address such misinformation as well as common stereotypes, which often serve as the primary driver of prejudice.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: While the survey highlighted that the vast majority of respondents affirmed that race or religion was not a barrier to social cohesion, it revealed some interesting findings which should be a cause for reflection and concern for us as a diverse and multi-ethnic society.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: This was higher than any other religious group, with a notable number staying in private housing.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: The hon Minister has spoken about the rise of Islamophobia over the years on multiple occasions.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: The recent IPS findings certainly reflect this concerning trend.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: As a society, it is not good enough to say that 85% of Singaporeans do not espouse such sentiments.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Worryingly, I also observed that many netizens online questioned the validity of the findings or simply dismissed it.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Just two days ago, Roses of Peace organised a youth forum titled, "Aftermath of Christchurch – Lessons for Singapore." About 120 youths participated in the session and we had a robust discussion on multiculturalism in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: The findings from the latest IPS study was a keen topic of discussion, and many of the youths found the findings troubling.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: There was a collective sense that, as a country and nation, we can do better.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: In this regard, I would like to raise some suggestions.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: First, to provide education of our diverse, multicultural social fabric.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: I believe more can be done to educate our youths from a young age on the various religious beliefs, ethnic traditions and cultural practices in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: We have such a rich cultural and social heritage that needs to be appreciated by all.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Beyond the common ties that bind us, we should also focus on helping our youths understand the unique elements of each faith traditions in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: At the same time, I urge the Government to equip our students with the necessary skillsets for effective dialogues and discussions on difficult and sensitive topics revolving around race and religion.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: This will help us be better mediators when occasional conflicts or disputes arise.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: We should also create more safe spaces in schools and the community where students are free to express their religious identity and for dialogues to take place in a mature and meaningful manner.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Second, dealing with spread of hate speech in the digital space.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: With the prevalence of smart phones and rise of extremist views that can disseminate rapidly online, the impact of hate speech is amplified.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Before the Christchurch attacks, the gunman published a manifesto on social media highlighting his extremist views.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: The livestreaming of the attacks further amplified the impact of these attacks.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: In addition to all the existing efforts, we must all focus on equipping society, especially our youths, with the tools and skills necessary to compete effectively with extreme voices in our new digital ecosystem.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: For example, we can develop a Digital Playbook to educate and equip fellow citizens with the knowledge and tools to counter hate speech and fake news.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Such a book can detail the strategies that ordinary citizens can adopt to identify and push back on such propaganda.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: This was first proposed at the United Nations (UN) General Assembly on 23 September 2010 by His Majesty King Abdullah II of Jordan.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: This week can be an occasion for us to celebrate the rich diversity of religions that harmoniously co-exist in Singapore and promote a deeper appreciation and tolerance through a series of exhibitions, performances and talks.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Singaporeans tend to treat discussions on religion as sensitive and potentially divisive.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: However, there is an imminent need to do more to bring such conversations to intersect with a wider societal audience.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: This is especially so in workplaces to foster better appreciation of people’s faiths, beliefs and to encourage employees to be proud of their identity.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: There is value for organisations to set aside one day in a year, perhaps during the Interfaith Harmony Week, to celebrate diversity in their workplaces.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore is the world's most religiously diverse country.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Multiculturalism, multi-religiosity and multiracialism are key tenets of our national values.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: However, to protect the peace and stability that we have, we need everyone to play a role and to play their part.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Everyone has a role in calling out hate speech and not being a silent bystander.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: We have been tireless in our efforts at building this precious social harmony over the past five decades.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Although we often claim that we are a work in progress, I hope Singapore will shine as a beacon of hope and serve as a role model to other nations struggling with social integration at the upcoming International Conference on Cohesive Societies.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Lastly, we cannot deepen racial and religious understanding without deepening our cultural understanding.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: (In Tamil):    In Singapore, we have to understand our culture very well so as to continuously remain as one united society, with racial and religious harmony.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: For instance, in the past 13 years, for the whole month of April, the Tamil Language Festival takes place.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Such language-based festivals not only help us nurture our mother tongue but also help us to understand our own culture better.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: To enhance racial and religious harmony, such festivals about mother tongue should take place continuously.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: (In English): Mr Deputy Speaker, with that, I thank Minister Shanmugam for moving the Motion and I support the Motion.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: These remarks are hurtful to Muslims, especially during a time of grief, expose an ignorance of the true Islamic faith and a lack of acknowledgment that terrorism does not choose its victims.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Many people all around the world condemned his insensitive remarks and some labelled his statement as hate speech.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: There were, however, those who appeared to show support for the Senator.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: This was highlighted in the commentary by Michael Yong featured by Channel NewsAsia, where the writer expressed concern regarding the nearly 10 petitions set up on Change.org, a popular petition site, to protect Anning's right to freedom of speech.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: He also referred to posts and groups standing "in solidarity" with Anning and calling for people to "respect his freedom of speech".

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The number of these groups of people may be relatively smaller and their views are not mainstream opinions.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Just last week in Singapore, IPS published a working paper on religion.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The findings of the survey, which were part of a global study, alluded to some worrying facts.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: There is an almost automatic perception that restriction is bad and would gnaw on our civil liberties.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Proponents of free speech often argue that it is a fundamental right.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: It is said that we need to allow for the marketplace of ideas to flourish and people should be allowed to come to their own conclusions about matters.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: In Singapore, there is a particular concern that the presence of many stringent rules would silence many, because of the fear of crossing the line.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: It limits open and meaningful discourse which may actually help clarify doubts and strengthen communal relations.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: We do need to embrace diversity of opinions and allow for a healthy discourse of even the most sensitive of issues.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: It leads to better understanding, and diversity can be a strength if ideas can be synergised and used for the good of the people.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: However, differences in views can also be a potential divisive factor that can tear our social fabric.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Worse, an extreme view, an expression that spreads, incites, promotes or justifies racial or religious hatred, can be damaging to a community.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: We, therefore, need a good framework in place that allows for open and candid discussions in safe spaces and for appropriate restrictions to be implemented to safeguard and protect our harmony.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I believe we also need a multi-pronged approach by having both legislation and education to address this issue.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: We need to also ensure that our people are edified, are sensible and sensitive, know what to reject and object to and that the right of free speech comes with responsibility and accountability for what is said.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: As a matter of principle, I believe there is general agreement amongst the public that we need to take effort to maintain racial and religious harmony in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Most people would agree that we should do this through education, through the creation of common spaces and opportunities for social bonding as well as the creation of safe spaces for meaningful discourse.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Many, possibly a lesser number, would agree that appropriate legislation needs to be in place to manage inappropriate conduct or expression that could incite racial or religious hatred.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Appropriate punishment deters unsavoury conduct and helps shape the society’s norms.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The difficulty is that what is expressed may lie in a spectrum of what is deemed hateful or offensive.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: If something said is offensive but falls short of being hateful, then what do we do?

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I do not think we can just let it slide.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: There must be a response as offensive speech also damages a society, albeit at a different pace.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: An indifference to something that is offensive can potentially normalise that expression in the long run and desensitise people to what is unacceptable.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I believe that there needs to still be some legislative restriction depending on the situation, but there needs to also be a whole lot of edification and an effort to sensitise the individual making the offensive speech to understand the harm he or she is causing to the community.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: On this note, I believe the approach taken with Imam Nalla some time back when he recited a supplication which offended the Jews and the Christians, was a correct one.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: He had to receive the punishment, but the resolution of the matter was done in a respectful manner and he apologised to the Christian leaders and the Rabbi.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: As we come across various instances of inappropriate conduct in the future, there needs to be a calibration and assessment of the harm done to the community.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: As we go down the spectrum of hateful and offensive expressions, we would reach the milder end of the expressions.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: There may be casual racism, inappropriate stereotype jokes, unspoken discomfort and even silent intolerance of another community.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I do not think it is practical or even meaningful to legislate regulations for these forms of conduct.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: But there is still a need to educate and allow for discourse.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: In this regard, I refer to another piece of finding from the recent IPS paper which I referred to earlier which has caused me great concern.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: But I think there is much that could be done to create opportunities for greater understanding and for strengthening interracial relations.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: (In Malay):   	I refer to the latest Working Paper by IPS.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: One of the published findings was about the percentage of Singaporeans that find Muslims threatening.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: This is certainly not the perception of the majority of respondents that were surveyed.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: However, to me, the number is not small.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: This is a reality that Muslims in Singapore have to overcome.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The issue of terrorism around the world and the past actions of ISIS to spread their message certainly had an impact on non-Muslims.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: We can decide how we want to face these issues.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: We can choose to feel anger or disappointment, but this will not change anything.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I think we can adopt a more positive approach by seeking opportunities to continue building good relations with the other communities in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: We can portray the true beauty of Islam and offer the hand of friendship to our fellow non-Muslim members of society.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I am confident that with this approach, the other communities will gain a better understanding of our religion and values.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: (In English): Mr Deputy Speaker, allow me to conclude in English.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: As a minority in Singapore, there are occasions when some things said or done by others from other races or religion may offend me or my community.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Often, such conduct comes from a space of ignorance and not malice.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: There is, therefore, a great need to continue to foster relations among people from different communities and allow for better understanding.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I am truly grateful though for the ability to practise my religion without fear for my safety.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I am truly grateful that many in the community can look beyond my tudung and embrace me for who I am.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: As I have shared in this House before, I grew up in the turbulent 1960s in Malaysia.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Those years were marred by several racial conflicts that saw many lives lost.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: There were curfews and, even as a kid, I could sense that something was wrong.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Sometimes, adults would gather and speak with low voices, their eyebrows furrowed.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: It is only because of our efforts to build racial and religious harmony that they have become much rarer today.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: It is easy to take harmony for granted.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: But, in fact, we face new challenges to maintaining harmony.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Over the world, there are people pursuing extremist ideologies.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: And because of our open society and the Internet, we hear of them through many sources.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: When you are influenced to hate a certain group, it is not a big jump to then take violent actions against that group.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: And once that happens, it will set off a cycle of hate and even more violence.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: We need to continue keeping our people safe.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Words can move emotion and give rise to hate, distrust and destruction.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: It takes weeks to create distrust and to sow the seeds of discontent.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: But it takes years and even generations to heal the wounds thereafter.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: If there is any suspicion that the law is not applied impartially, it will sow discord among groups.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Do not spread in your community that the rules are not applied fairly.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: That is a very dangerous perception and will spread faster than you think.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: When the information is clarified, it will not spread as far as the original rumour.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Especially if you are a public figure or an influencer, be very careful on such matters.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I feel some senior Singaporeans, who have been through the mayhem of riots, can put their experience to good use.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: (In Mandarin):   	We will not tolerate anyone who spread hate speech against any race or religion.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Hate speech can influence people and they might stage an attack on other races and religions.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: This will severely harm our racial and religious harmony and even result in a series of revenge actions.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: In Singapore, we will be applying the law impartially to protect all racial and religious groups.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: If you hear anyone making hate speech against a certain community, please report to the Police so that MHA will have time to investigate and take actions.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Do not spread words among the community that MHA did not take any action.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Such kind of rumours spreads very quickly and it is very dangerous.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Some Singaporeans have been through the mayhem of riots.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I hope the Government can invite them to share their experiences so that every Singaporean can understand why there is a need to resist hate speech.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: (In English): Mr Deputy Speaker, Sir, in the end, we just need to remember one thing.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Hate speech goes against the founding principles of Singapore to be one united people, regardless of race, language or religion.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: We need to take a firm stand against it.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The first is on non-fundamentalist approach to freedom of speech and expression; the second, our pre-emptive approach to hate speech legislation, and the last, a warning against toothless legislation.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The Guardian newspaper argued that in Britain, editorial decisions have always been guided, not just by law, but by a sense of "what is fair and tolerable within British society".

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The press in Singapore here, too, did not publish the cartoons.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Further, the version of The Economist which was distributed in Singapore had the cartoon redacted.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Tribal instincts cannot be eradicated, nor should we want to.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The irrationality of love is matched, and often outmatched, by the irrationality of hate.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Even as we promote our best selves, we must constrain our worst.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We do this softly through education, moral suasion and social norms.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: But we must also do this with unequivocal force through the smite of laws and their strict enforcement.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: This law has been revised over the years to include language that is deemed to incite "racial and religious hatred", as well as "hatred on the grounds of sexual orientation" and language that "encourages terrorism".

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: In 2016, the European Union (EU) established the Code of Conduct, as a push for social media platforms to crack down on hate speech.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Subsequently, four giant information technology (IT) companies – Google+, Instagram, Snapchat and Dailymotion – decided to join the EU "Code of Conduct on countering illegal hate speech online".

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Our Home Affairs Minister has pointed out the relatively lax legislation both in the UK and the US.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: This is not because they do not see hate speech as wrong, but because they see freedom of expression as right.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Two wrongs do not make a right, but what do two rights make?

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: When the right to freedom of expression is fundamental, and the right to freedom of religious belief is fundamental, what do we do?

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The extreme liberal approach is to do nothing and let the two fundamentals contest in the open.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We cannot leave it to the law of the jungle.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We cannot say, "This is not a government problem.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Let the people sort it out among themselves." We must say, as we are doing today, "This is allowed in the public space – and that is not." Our laws must provide guidance on the clash of rights, not just in Court but in everyday life.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: This is my first point about the non-fundamentalist nature of our approach to freedom of expression.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: My second point relates to hate speech legislation and the degree to which it should be regulated.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: I mentioned about the Charlie Hebdo incident and Singapore's strong stance against publishing images offensive to members of our community.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: In this case, because of the tragic murder, there were few critics of what we did.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: But remember that we had censored the images in advance of the shootings.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We did so because it was wrong, and the nature of this "wrong" is that it is against the norms of what we stand for, as well as the possible harms that could arise.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: In most cases, the actions we take are in advance of these harms, that is, we take a pre-emptive approach to minimise harm.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: This opens us up to criticism of being overly authoritarian, of infantilising the public, or not respecting people's ability to govern, control or decide for themselves.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Why so hypersensitive? "What is the harm?", people asked.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We may be able to outline these harms, but if we do our job well, the public may never experience them, and hence, never believe that the risk of such harm was real.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: This creates a very different kind of problem.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: And this brings me to my last point about whether we ought to enforce our laws relating to hate speech strictly or loosely.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The second method allows people to experience harm in small measure and, by the logic of vaccination, builds up our resilience and ability to debate contested ideas.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: I agree that contestation of ideas and debate is valuable in many areas, but relating to this body of legislation, I argue for a strict application.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The point has been made by the Minister for Home Affairs – the nature of law flows to the nature of the country.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We, in this House, can choose whether we want to be more proactive and tough in the applications of our laws, especially when these are extended to new hard cases.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: So, I would rather be conservative and safe than experimental and sorry.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Many older societies have seen the fractures, fissures and wounds which, once opened up, are hard to heal, especially on matters relating to race and religion.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Strong enforcement will also provide deterrent effects because knowing that the Government is serious about enforcement has real consequences on behaviour, both among the people and corporations.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We see this in the continued existence of hate speech, instances of clear violations that persist with impunity.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Australia, for example, does not have a strong record of confronting white nationalism.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: In recent years, we see Government senators voting for a motion that it is "okay to be white".

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: A flexible enforcement of laws may be one way of coping with the clash of two fundamentals but, as I have said before, it is not Singaporeans' way.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Ours is a more difficult, more rigid and, some would say, less liberal model.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: This may indeed be so, but it is a choice that does not denigrate freedoms in general, but instead, respects as many freedoms as possible.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: It certainly does not place the freedom to express hate over the freedom to practise one's religion.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Such instincts create mistrust, hostility and, as we have seen in recent days, death and dissolution.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: But our tribal instinct also creates heroes, when the best among us strives to protect the rest, when we see altruism, kindness, fair play, duty and sacrifice.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We cannot legislate heroism, no more than we can outlaw villainy.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: But we can and must use laws to give the best chance for our ambitions to do good, and to constrain, deter and severely punish those who plan to do evil.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Minister for Social and Family Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: When this means excluding communities and fracturing our society, it is a cost that we cannot bear.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Minister for Social and Family Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: In its simplest form, hate speech can manifest in a single tweet or a passing comment.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Minister for Social and Family Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Yet, malicious content and intent can easily create unfounded fear and suspicion.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Minister for Social and Family Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: With the expansion of new platforms, hate speech can now come in numerous forms of expression which proliferates, incites or legitimises any form of hatred based on intolerance.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Minister for Social and Family Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: In a multicultural state like Singapore, it is inevitable that societal fault lines exist.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Minister for Social and Family Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: However, hate speech exploits and deepens these fault lines, creating an echo chamber, polarising our society, and threatens the very essence of our existence.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Minister for Social and Family Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: It has become increasingly apparent that extremist groups on both ends of the spectrum feed off each other’s intolerance.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Minister for Social and Family Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: By doing so, they create animosity where there was none, suspicion which was previously absent and divisions in place of unity.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Minister for Social and Family Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: With the increased prevalence of hate speech and efforts to curb it, our society now begins to question whether the provisions we have are sufficient or even necessary.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Minister for Social and Family Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Where does hate speech begin and how can we terminate its progression?

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Minister for Social and Family Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Seemingly innocuous offensive comments may lead to the development of hate speech.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Minister for Social and Family Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Yet, it is difficult to draw a definitive line as to what should be banned or not.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Minister for Social and Family Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: This is particularly because offensive speech exists on a continuum of varying levels of hostility.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Minister for Social and Family Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Hence, it is pertinent that such cases still be evaluated on a case-by-case basis to consider the context and content of such statements.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Minister for Social and Family Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: A similar challenge faced in eradicating hate speech is its prevalence in different mediums.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Minister for Social and Family Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Music, in particular, is an effective platform to instil and spread notions of animosity.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Minister for Social and Family Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Music can be weaponised as it easily desensitises one to hateful perceptions.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Minister for Social and Family Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: The frequent exposure to such themes in unconventional genres can legitimise and deepen intolerance.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Minister for Social and Family Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Whilst we may think of our multiracial and multi-religious harmony as a delicate balance that needs to be protected, there is room for constructive efforts to strengthen our community's resilience in facing hate.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Minister for Social and Family Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Within our local community, artists can provide a countervailing narrative towards hate speech.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Minister for Social and Family Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: In this way, music can be utilised to deepen interactions and strengthen our community.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Minister for Social and Family Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: In my role in the Malay Language Council and Malay Language Learning and Promotion Committee, I have engaged many professionals in the music, art and literature fraternities.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Minister for Social and Family Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Amongst these individuals, I am pleased to share that there is a resounding rejection against music, art and literature that purported hateful sentiments.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Minister for Social and Family Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: (In Malay):   	In the Malay community, our identity is reflected in our community's traditional practices or in the way we portray ourselves to the other communities.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Minister for Social and Family Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Hate speech will only isolate and segregate the minority communities.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Minister for Social and Family Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: In our daily actions and conduct, we should rightly display empathy and kindness.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Minister for Social and Family Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: By doing so, we can reject any hate statement that has no basis whatsoever.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Minister for Social and Family Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: At the same time, we must not be influenced by those who want to fan the flames of hatred between us and the other communities.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Minister for Social and Family Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: We must be aware of their evil intentions that will only serve to separate us from other Singaporeans.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Minister for Social and Family Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Graciousness and civility form the core of our identity.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Minister for Social and Family Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: These values remind us that hate speech contradicts the principles that we adhere to.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Minister for Social and Family Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: We must not get involved in spreading hate speech through social media.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Minister for Social and Family Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: It is our responsibility to counter such false statements.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Minister for Social and Family Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: There is a Malay saying, "When you pinch the left thigh, the right thigh feels painful too" and, thus, we must be sensitive to the well-being of those who become targets of hate speech.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Minister for Social and Family Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: In our effort to fight hate speech together, we must build our resilience against statements tinged with hatred.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Minister for Social and Family Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Through literature, the arts and music, we can send messages or reminders that promote cohesion.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Minister for Social and Family Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Among all the platforms that are available to us, music is most prominent as the unifying tool that can counter influences that promote enmity.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Minister for Social and Family Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Music activists that I have approached have unanimously rejected aspects of hate speech in their lyrics, songs and performances.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Minister for Social and Family Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: These activists, who come from different backgrounds and comprise young and experienced musicians, say that the music they play contain positive elements and support the cohesion and development of society and nation.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Minister for Social and Family Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Another specific example from our community is the Dikir Barat performance which we can use to counter hate speech.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Minister for Social and Family Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Mr Djohan Abdul Rahman, the founder of the Andika Kencana group, as well as the former president of the Dikir Barat Federation and member of ASAS' 50 shared with me that "Lyrics play an important role in any Dikir Barat performance.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Minister for Social and Family Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Therefore, negative lyrics that fan the flames of hatred and violence will have a negative impact on the arts community." These influences will spread to other arts activists and participants who are accustomed to such themes through rehearsals and performances.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Minister for Social and Family Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Therefore, Dikir Barat lyrics promote a harmonious living environment and sharing of experiences and shared values.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Minister for Social and Family Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Dikir Barat activists have consciously strived to strengthen social cohesion as a weapon to counter hate sentiments.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Minister for Social and Family Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Cikgu Suratman Markasan, a recipient of the Cultural Medallion, as well as a Tun Sri Lanang Award winner and an important figure in the Southeast Asia Literary Council (Mastera), pointed out that literary works promoting hatred towards other communities do not represent values that are present in the Malay culture and, therefore, should not be encouraged or read.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Minister for Social and Family Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: There is a song by Ramli Sarip, where the lyrics go like this: "Listen not to false poetry Because it will tarnish your soul Listen to poetry that we inherited Passed down through the generations until today." His song carries the theme of brotherhood and love for one another.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Minister for Social and Family Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Certainly, these are the values that we should promote.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Minister for Social and Family Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: (In English): Allow me to continue my speech in English.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Minister for Social and Family Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Besides removing hate speech from our media platforms, the best protection against hateful sentiments is the strength of the community.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Minister for Social and Family Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: This is because hate speech is not just a means of expression but a reflection of deeper attitudes and perceptions.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Minister for Social and Family Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: To make our communities less susceptible to the manipulation of such hateful narratives, we need to increase the depth of our cross-cultural and religious exchanges.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Minister for Social and Family Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: It comes in the most proximate groups of people we interact with, that is, our neighbours, colleagues and peers.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Minister for Social and Family Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: It is important to deepen such relations to gain a personal understanding of the cultures and customs of different peoples.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Minister for Social and Family Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Recognise that tolerance and understanding are not enough to deter hate; trust is what we need.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Minister for Social and Family Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: This is especially pertinent, given that trust is not a given in a multicultural society.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Minister for Social and Family Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: While in this case it reveals how continuous and heightened reporting of terrorism by some in the name of Islam has brought out misgivings about the Muslims in Singapore, more importantly, it indicates that more than just being inclusive, our communities need to build confidence and trust with one another.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Minister for Social and Family Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: This work is never done because every incident causes a backslide.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Minister for Social and Family Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: This building of trust starts from home, too.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Minister for Social and Family Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: When our children have their first interactions with others from different races or religions, it helps for us to guide them along and answer their queries.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Minister for Social and Family Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: More importantly, we should encourage a sense of empathy in our children to humanise Singaporeans from different racial and religious groups.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Minister for Social and Family Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: It can come in the little things – inviting their friends over for festivals or advising against any hateful comments spreading on social media.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Minister for Social and Family Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: As their closest advisors, we provide the next generation the way forward in the uncertain terrain of these times, often ridden with hate.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Minister for Social and Family Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: I call upon all my Parliamentary colleagues and fellow Singaporeans in making this pledge.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Minister for Social and Family Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: To deny its influence, there must be a common conviction against intolerance.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Minister for Social and Family Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: This means standing up for groups that are targeted by hate speech.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Minister for Social and Family Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: This means providing comfort for others who feel alienated.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Minister for Social and Family Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: This means feeling for others even though we belong to a different race or religious group.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Minister for Social and Family Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: The challenge of hate speech means our community needs to move beyond being understanding and tolerant.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Minister for Social and Family Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
