text: We are now called upon to support, protect and defend one another.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think the collective position of this House is clear.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Offensive speech can segue into hate speech, can overlap and, if we allow offensive speech into religion, politics, media, entertainment, the tone and texture of public discourse will change.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think there is broad support, based on the speeches, for the approach that I have outlined, and it is very heartening that Government Members of Parliament, Opposition, Nominated Members of Parliament broadly agreed to these principles.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Pritam Singh asked some questions about the processes between IMDA and MHA.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I have explained that in some detail in my opening speech.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: MHA withdrew its objections, as I explained earlier.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: A few days later – I think two days later – MHA gave advice to cancel.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And I have explained that also at quite some length just earlier.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Pritam Singh also asked about the reasons for cancellation of the concert.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Again, I do not think he wants me to go into the detail that I have given in my opening speech.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think the Member broadly agrees with the principles, but he had a question on the cancellation of Watain, specifically.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He accepted that he was not aware of the opposition of mainstream Christian viewpoint.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And now that I have explained that to him, I think he will appreciate that, and, in turn, that is relevant for the broader security considerations and assessment as well in the way that I explained in my opening speech.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And I think the Member would accept that it then becomes a question of judgement.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Pritam Singh also made some comparisons with bands in the past.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think in all of these things, the population, the reactions are dynamic.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We have to assess it with the facts we have and not be wishful about what it was, and what it might be in the distant future.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, population, reactions, specific bands, time period – these are all relevant considerations.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You have to make an honest assessment based on all of those with the reactions that you have, whether it is mainstream reaction, and how it would impact on specific security situations as well as the broader security considerations.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: IMDA, in fact, has to make a series of decisions – tough calls – on a broad variety of issues going well beyond the security issues.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I would say security stricto sensu is, in fact, the easier issue, compared with the kind of issues IMDA has to deal with when faced with any kind of application.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And it is not as if MCI wanted to proceed in any event, or that it was unaware of security considerations.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But, here, it is understandable that MHA picked it up – our agencies' primary job is to keep in touch, close touch, with the religious communities, the leaders; we picked up on the mainstream Christian opinion within a day or so, made the security call, and discussed it with MCI.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I would add that this does not mean that there is any general ban on black metal groups – I think that was a point either the Member asked or sort of implied.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Now, let me turn to Mr Murali Pillai.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He asked how to deprive commercial entities from making money and spreading hate speech.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think the points he made are valid; they need to be considered.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And I think there were specific points on MRHA and ISA, and the extent of Government powers.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I would say it has worked well so far.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Government's exercise of powers has been understood, and the constraints on the Government's exercise of power and safeguards in the legislation as well as in the Constitution have been understood.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Ms Denise Phua asked what constitutes offensive speech.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We do not intervene in disagreements or arguments on public issues on WhatsApp and other platforms.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I cannot tell you that I have all the answers on those issues.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But we will have to deal with them.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: On enforcement, the Member asked about existing legislation and how we would fairly debate the approach.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As I explained, the purpose of this debate is not to enforce something specifically.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is to set out the approach, clarify our approach, hear Members of Parliament again, have it debated.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And then, hopefully with that, the population will also understand what the people's representatives are saying here, and what kind of approach we take.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Christopher de Souza, Senior Parliamentary Secretary Sun Xueling, Mr Saktiandi Supaat, Ms Joan Pereira, Er Dr Lee Bee Wah, Senior Parliamentary Secretary Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim, Mr Seah Kian Peng – we note their comments have been broadly supportive.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They talked about how hate speech travels and how it fuels violence.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah spoke about her personal experiences.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Likewise, we heard from the perspective of the minority community Members of Parliament.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And Mr Seah Kian Peng's points on being conservative when it comes to this specific area, I think accords with what our society believes in and heels to the kind of approach that we have set out.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And I thank her for the points that she made.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We do need to tackle hate speech online.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I will say that we are very far from tackling it today.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Nominated Member of Parliament Terence Ho made a number of points on the space for arts.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I do not think there is any disagreement on that, that there should be cultural vibrancy.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Those are the questions I raised for this debate.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The points that he has raised more broadly on cultural vibrancy, I do not think affect the narrower set of points I have made, and I do not think he disagrees with me.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira made a very thoughtful speech.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He made the point, tracing through the history of Islam and Christianity that is central to religion.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He talked about Jesus, Martin Luther, the Prophet – all led movements to change.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Insofar as that is relevant to today's debate, I would say I cannot and I will not argue against that point, but also, I think the state has no role in either fomenting such change within religion or supporting one side or the other.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The second point the Member made was that religion should not impose its views on public policy.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I will take that with the third point he made, that there has been a greater public assertion of fate.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In fact, the point that I think he is seeking to make but perhaps did not put it quite so directly, is that if you give in to these greater public assertions of faith, and if people of religion become extremely sensitive, then there is a risk of cutting down public space.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And also something that he did not quite mention but flows from it – a political leadership which is not strong enough to stand on its two feet and seeks favours from particular religious groups or specific religious groups.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It happens in many countries, including those in this region.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That will lead to a different type of government and public policymaking and it will not be a secular government.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: People may be influenced by their religious outlook, but you do not make public policy based on a particular religious outlook, or a particular standpoint of a particular religion.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Then, you will lose the faith of everybody else in society of a different outlook.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That has never been our position, and as long as the Government holds true to the values that have been set out, which I will not go into, then I think we will avoid that risk.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is a risk because so many governments, both in this region and outside, have gone down that route.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is one of the easiest ways to get votes.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, we have to make sure that we seek understanding among the religious groups, mutual respect with religious leaders in a multi-religious society.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But I would suggest to Assoc Prof Walter Theseira that that is perhaps a topic for another debate on another day, another Ministerial Statement, or the Member of Parliament can move a Motion.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Minister Grace Fu spoke about not just the rules, but also the need to make sure that we work very hard to make sure that our multi-religious approach works.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: On 22 March 2019, at a Memorial Service in Christchurch, this was what he said, and I am not going to read all of it, just some passages: "Brothers and sisters in Islam, brothers and sisters in humanity, brothers and sisters in New Zealand.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Last Friday, I stood in this mosque and saw hatred and rage in the eyes of the terrorist, who killed and martyred 50 people, wounded 42 and broke the hearts of millions around the world.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Today, from the same place, I look out and see the love and compassion in the eyes of thousands of fellow New Zealanders, fellow human beings from across the globe that have filled the hearts of millions more who are not with us physically but in spirit.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This terrorist sought to tear our nation apart with an evil ideology that has torn the world apart.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But, instead, we have shown that New Zealand is unbreakable.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And that the world can see in us an example of love and unity.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We are brokenhearted but we are not broken.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We are determined not to let anyone divide us.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The number of people killed is not extraordinary but the solidarity in New Zealand is extraordinary.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Families of the victims, your loved ones did not die in vain.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Through them, the world will see the beauty of Islam and the beauty of our unity.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We are here in our hundreds and thousands unified for one purpose – that hate will be undone and love will redeem us.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is a targeted campaign to influence people to dehumanise and irrationally fear Muslims.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: To fear what we wear, to fear the choice of food we eat, to fear the way we pray and to fear the way we practise our faith.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We call upon governments around the world, including New Zealand and the neighbouring countries, to bring an end to hate speech and the politics of fear.
